entities.title: Lady Frostwhisker
entities.content:
Lady Frostwhisker is a silver-blue grande dame of the middle rank who has spent twenty years conducting the most patient campaign in Mayfur: the elevation of her house from good to great by means of entertainments nobody can afford to miss. She is not the ton's most powerful hostess, the Dowager and the Duchess of Fluffington hold the summits, but she is its most inventive, and her calendar is where the season goes to be surprised: the musicale that gave the diamond question its most quoted retreat, the winter skating party the year the Saucerine obliged by freezing, and now the Venetian breakfast, which will be remembered longer than she intended and for reasons she did not choose.

Her method is detail. The Frostwhisker events are planned like campaigns, provisioned like sieges, and reviewed afterward with her steward line by line, an practice the ton would find mercantile if the results were not so reliably splendid. Her one blind spot, cats who know her agree, is that she plans for everything except high spirits, her own youth having been conducted entirely indoors.

She bore the wreck of the breakfast with a composure that earned her more standing than the breakfast itself would have: one look at the wading Ambassador, one at the sinking punt, and she announced, in a carrying voice, that the entertainment had concluded precisely as rehearsed and the swimming was by subscription only. The ton laughed, the crisis died, and Lady Whiskerdown's number that week awarded her the season's palm for presence of mind, which she has had framed.

entities.title: Miss Frostwhisker
entities.content:
Miss Frostwhisker is the season's cautionary footnote on the subject of crossing the ward of Blackfriars. A pretty, quick-tongued silver kitten with her mother's eye for effect and none of her patience, she opened her first season by remarking, at her own family's musicale, that farm manners were this year's novelty and would be next year's embarrassment. The remark travelled, as remarks at musicales do, and within the week Miss Frostwhisker's invitation to the Blackfriars at-home had been withdrawn, mislaid, the household said, with regret, in a tone that closed the subject.

What makes her interesting, rather than merely instructive, is what she did next. Having taken the measure of the mistake, she neither sulked nor campaigned; she called at Grimalkin Square, unannounced, was received, the Square holds its breath even now retelling it, and apologised, plainly, without an audience to perform for. What was said in return nobody knows, but the two young ladies were seen the following Wednesday sharing a lemonade at Almeow's with every appearance of treaty, and the trailing end of a certain ribbon, which the knot-readers had confidently predicted, never appeared.

The ton concluded that the Frostwhisker girl had more of her mother in her than the remark suggested. The better observers concluded something more useful: that the ward of Blackfriars keeps her reversals for cats who will not learn, and banks the ones who will, and that Miss Frostwhisker is now, by the season's oddest route, inside the youngest and most watchable alliance in Town.

entities.title: The Venetian Breakfast
entities.content:
Lady Frostwhisker's Venetian breakfast was to be the season's most original entertainment: the Saucerine dressed as a lagoon, a flotilla of punts poled by footmen, tables at the water's edge, and the ton afloat by mid-morning on the understanding that Venice is chiefly a matter of confidence. For one golden hour it worked, and the hostesses of Mayfur were privately drafting their imitations.

Then young Lord Frisk, poling with more conviction than instruction, took his punt across the wake of another, overcorrected with his whole heart, and delivered himself, the punt, and the luncheon service of table six broadside into the shallows. The wave that followed was modest by nautical standards and biblical by social ones: eleven tablecloths drowned, a tier of ices lost with all hands, and the hat of His Excellency the Ambassador from the Kingdom of Dogs lifted from his head and borne away with, witnesses swear, a certain dignity, toward the carp.

His Excellency laughed until he required assistance. Lady Frostwhisker pronounced the entertainment concluded as rehearsed. And the ton, which forgives originality nothing, had its verdict on the boy ready by supper: rusticated, ruined, done. The season, as it turned out, had other plans for him, but that is the affair of a later number; the breakfast itself passed into the language at once, and no entertainment since has been proposed near open water without somebody murmuring that at least it cannot go worse than Venice.

entities.title: The Foreclosure Week
entities.content:
The first week of August, the arithmetic the whole season had priced finally moved: the house of Manxfield called the Fluffington paper. Notices went through attorneys of the unhurried kind, the wagering at Brindle's compressed two years of speculation into five days of settlement, and Mayfur arranged its face for the crash it had rehearsed so long that several hostesses had already planned the condolence dinners.

The week's true drama ran below the ton's line of sight, in the sequence the arithmeticians could not price. Mr. Bobtail, holding at last every respectable claim on the silver house, stood at the summit of the most patient revenge in the herring trade's history, with the ton waiting to learn what forty years of counting looked like when it finally spent itself. What it looked like, the Monday following at his own at-home, was a father crossing his drawing room to hand three notes to his daughter, and the season's whole ledger changing character in the time it takes paper to burn.

The week is already passing into Brindle's lore as the great anticlimax, which the better heads in that institution dispute: the crash, they point out, was real, and it landed, and what it landed on was not the cat the town had gathered to watch fall. The other creditor east of the wall, whose paper was senior and whose interest was never payable in coin, discovered by Friday that events had quietly repossessed his security's usefulness, and the east, which does not attend at-homes, closed its own book on the coat with a shrug the west end will never hear and would not survive hearing.

entities.title: The Forgiveness at Manxfield
entities.content:
On the second Monday of August, at an at-home of some forty guests, the season produced the scene it will be remembered by. Mr. Bobtail rose without announcement, unlocked the strongbox that half of Brindle's had wagered on, and gave the three notes of Fluffington debt to his daughter, saying nothing at all, which cats who know him call the longest speech of his life. Miss Beatrice Bobtail took her ally Miss Longwhisker by the paw, walked the notes to the fire, and fed them in.

Her sentence to the room is already in the season's book of quotations: that the ladies had discussed what his lordship's fourteen generations were worth, and had decided they should all rather learn what he was worth without them; that he owed them nothing; that he never had; and that the debt was always somebody else's idea of what they were owed. The room did not recover its conversation for ten minutes. The Duchess of Fluffington, present by a courtesy nobody had expected her to accept, sat very still through the whole of it, and left early, and sent, the following morning, to Manxfield, a single card on which was written, in a fine old-fashioned slanting hand, one word: taught.

What the fire ended is countable: a foreclosure, two years of wagering, the marriage-market siege of two households. What it began has kept the ton up at night since, because mercy on that scale, spent in public by the two cats with the best claim to withhold it, reorganises a town's whole arithmetic of grievance, and Mayfur is not sure it can afford the exchange rate. The two ladies, asked everywhere since to explain themselves, decline everywhere, with the same composure they learned, the ton now remembers, in the same hard school.

entities.title: The Shearing
entities.content:
For two years the coat was the question of Mayfur, and in the end Mayfur was not even in the room when it was answered. In the days after the fire at Manxfield, Lord Fluffington vanished from the town's sight altogether, no clubs, no calls, no sightings at any window, and the ton, cheated of its crash and now of its subject, was reduced to theories, of which it produced eleven, all wrong.

He reappeared at the season's last ball, and the entrance is already the stuff of Almeow's legend: the great silver argument of Mayfur gone entire, clipped to the plain grey cat beneath, correctly dressed in one good coat of the woven kind, walking into the first rooms in the kingdom the way cats walk into cold water, all at once, having decided. The room took its breath and held it. And then, near the mantel, a paw began to tap, and the sound spread, and what moved through the ballroom was not applause, Almeow's does not applaud, but something older: the sound of a wall deciding, all in one moment, to be a door.

What the town has been told is nothing, which is why the town has finally, two years too late, understood the coat: it was never a vanity. It was a collateral, a livery, and a cage, and the cat inside it has walked out and left it to the birds. He danced once, with Miss Longwhisker, and gave the season its epitaph when she asked how he did: lighter, madam, and learning the weather. The wagering interest, denied every crash it priced, has opened a book on his prospects, and for the first time in fourteen generations the odds on a Fluffington are kind.

entities.title: The Diamond Decision
entities.content:
Between the second dance and the supper interval of the mid-August ball, the patronesses of Almeow's ended the season's great contest with the timing of professionals who had been enjoying themselves: the diamond of the season is Miss Marigold, ward of Blackfriars, born in a barn at Foldingworth and arrived, by way of one ruby ribbon and the most patiently constructed campaign in the institution's memory, at the exact centre of the world.

The moment the room remembers is not the announcement but the two responses. The new diamond received it with a curtsey of textbook depth and eyes, for once, exactly the size nature made them, which the connoisseurs note was itself the campaign's final move: triumph worn as modesty is triumph doubled. And Her Highness the Princess Lilac, the retiring holder, who had declined all season to acknowledge that any contest existed, inclined her head to her successor by precisely the degree the occasion required, resumed her conversation with the Ambassador in her own tongue, and the following morning sent to the west side of the Square, without a card, a single lilac bloom.

Town has produced eleven readings of the bloom and will winter on them. The new diamond placed it in water in her own window, facing the Square, where it stood until the knockers came off, and the two finest campaigners in Mayfur are understood to require no translation. The wager book settled at sums the committee has asked the papers not to print; the papers, feeling the season had been hard enough on that institution, complied; and the knot of the ruby ribbon, the whole town notes, has been a plain bow ever since, all quiet, which the fleet-watchers refuse to believe means the fleet is home.

entities.title: The Mews, No. 1: a sheet for the counting class
entities.content:
Gentle kitchens,

This sheet is for us. It will be chalked when there is matter, copied while the copper heats, and gone by the fish, and it will concern itself with the only news that was ever any use below the pavement: what things cost, what work is owed, and who pays.

In this first number, the spring wage table, east terrace, entered plain. One house pays above the rate and to the hour, and every kitchen on the Walk knows which. Three pay the rate. Two pay the rate in promises, and one of those two has begun paying the promises in smaller promises, and the sheet will return to that house at quarter-day with the table updated and the arrears totalled, because an arrear written down plainly has a way of embarrassing itself into coin.

Also in this number: the fish, honest at Sweep's stalls and creative elsewhere, prices below; the price of a link-boy's coat against a single ballroom candle, arithmetic the reader may finish personally; and notice that the dairy board will carry, henceforth, the standing list of houses that charge their girls for candle ends, until the practice stops, which, gentle kitchens, it now will.

You ask who I am. Ask instead why the tradesman's entrance sees everything and is never once looked at. I am the entrance. Doors are the honest half of every house, and it is time the honest half kept a page.

Swept and locked,
THE AREA CAT

entities.title: The Mews: on the biscuits of record
entities.content:
Gentle kitchens,

The west end's oldest joke is the refreshments at a certain assembly rooms, and on Wednesday last a young gentleman of fashion was heard to declare, at the hatch itself, that the lemonade was an insult to his subscription. The sheet has decided the joke is old enough to retire, and will retire it with arithmetic, gently, and no further than this: the table allowance of that institution, set by its foundresses at a figure worthy of the rooms, is spent to about a fifth of its weight on the famous biscuit, and the difference, gentle kitchens, is spent, quarterly, in full, exactly where you would spend it, and has been for longer than any patroness now living can say, and the sheet declines to embarrass either the biscuit or the board by itemising a farthing further.

The young gentleman may keep his joke. The sheet suggests only that he make it more quietly at the hatch, where the staff eat after him, hot, first, and without complaint, by an arrangement of the door's own keeping that is also nobody's business, and also entered here, initials only, P., with the sheet's compliments.

Prices this week: whiting up a penny on the late tides, candles steady, lye dear again and the court advises buying short. And the east terrace arrears table, updated: one house has cleared to March, which the sheet enters with pleasure, pleasure being rarer on that page than coin.

Swept and locked,
THE AREA CAT

entities.title: Dominic, Duke of Blackfriars
entities.content:
The Duke of Blackfriars was born, as the wags of Brindle's never tire of observing, already dressed for the evening: black from ears to haunches, with a white shirtfront and white gloves so crisp that no valet in Mayfur can improve upon them. He is a big cat, heavy in the shoulder, and he moves through a ballroom the way a barge moves through smaller traffic, slowly, and with the absolute confidence that everything else will make way.

What the newer debutantes do not know, and what the older toms remember very well, is that His Grace was once the Friar, the most feared bare-claw fighter the pits of the Rookery ever produced. He does not speak of those years. He has, in his own phrase, handed the ring to the next generation, and now fights only with his silences, which are considerable. Cats bring him their disputes because his judgments are fair to a fault; he has ruled against his own house twice, and both times dared anyone present to remark upon it.

He is gentleness itself with kittens, with the elderly, and above all with his ward, Miss Marigold, who has him wrapped entirely around one calico paw and knows it. But the ton keeps one rule the way it keeps no other: do not touch the cats the Duke loves. The last gentleman who tried is said to have taken up residence in Bath, permanently, and at short notice.

entities.title: The Dowager Countess of Nalewood
entities.content:
The Dowager Countess of Nalewood has outlived three earls, two wars, and every cat who ever thought her finished. Her eyes clouded to moonstone years ago, and she has not once needed them since. She navigates Town by whisker, memory, and the sound of other cats' evasions, which she hears at forty paces. She carries a thin silver-tipped stick, not to find her way, but to rap the ankles of anyone who says something foolish in her presence, and Mayfur's ankles are, as a class, bruised.

She is the true matriarch of the ton. Invitations are not final until Nalewood has accepted or declined; matches are not made until she has sniffed the pedigree; and reputations she has decided to protect simply do not fall, however hard the season pulls at them. The Duke of Blackfriars, who defers to no living creature, defers to her. When asked why, he is reported to have said only: she was fair to me before it was fashionable.

The Dowager reads Lady Whiskerdown's Society Papers aloud to her companions every morning it appears, or rather, has it read to her, and corrects it. Her corrections are never wrong. There are cats in Mayfur who believe she knows exactly who Lady Whiskerdown is, and has her own reasons for keeping the secret. The Dowager, asked directly, smiled and said that blindness has made her an excellent keeper of things unseen.

entities.title: Princess Lilac of Siam
entities.content:
Princess Lilac arrived in Town two seasons ago with a retinue of four, a wardrobe of nothing (she has observed that her coat required eleven generations of breeding and cannot be purchased on Ribbon Row), and a bloodline that runs, by way of a Tonkin grandmother, directly back to the palace cats of Siam. She is, and there is no argument to be had about it, the most beautiful creature in Mayfur: lilac point, cream and smoke, with lines a sculptor would weep over and the musculature of an athlete under all that elegance. She holds the standing record for the Almeow's mantel leap, set casually, in a single motion, while continuing a conversation.

She is also, the ton whispers, entirely aware of all of the above. The Princess does not enter rooms; she permits rooms to receive her. Her voice is the other thing no one forgets: the true carrying voice of Siam, capable of reaching three ballrooms and a cloakroom, deployed without mercy when she is displeased, which is often.

She was named diamond of the season the day she arrived, and held the title unchallenged until a certain calico ward of the Duke of Blackfriars began her extraordinary campaign. The Princess has declined to acknowledge the rivalry, which is how everyone knows it is real.

entities.title: Lady Tabitha of Blackfriars
entities.content:
Lady Tabitha, tabby and white, is the Duke of Blackfriars' younger sister, and the season's most reliable source of alarm. She has courage the way other cats have fleas: abundantly, and to the discomfort of everyone nearby. What she does not have, by her own cheerful admission, is any particular plan. She takes her chances because taking chances is how she has always survived, and it has worked so far, by margins that grow narrower every season.

Her catalogue of near-ruin is long. She has fallen into the Saucerine twice, both times from railings she had been expressly told not to walk. She entered the gentlemen's wager book at Brindle's under an assumed name and won. She was seen at midnight on the Saucerine bridge with a large ginger gentleman of criminal reputation, an incident her brother has forbidden the ton to mention and which the ton therefore mentions constantly.

She is impossible to discipline because she receives every scolding as applause. The Dowager Countess of Nalewood once delivered her a dressing-down of legendary severity, and Tabitha is reported to have purred through the whole of it and asked whether there was more. Her brother despairs of her. Her brother would also, and everyone knows this too, burn Town to the ground for her.

entities.title: Miss Marigold, Ward of Blackfriars
entities.content:
Miss Marigold came to Grimalkin Square from Foldingworth Farm looking like something out of a painting: a small cloud of calico fluff with enormous eyes, resembling nothing so much as the kitten of some vast and noble longhair line. Half of Mayfur assumed she was exactly that. She has never corrected them. She was, in fact, born in a barn, third of six, and learned everything she knows about power from watching which cat got the warm spot by the dairy door.

What Miss Marigold understands, and what her rivals learn too late, is that cuteness is not a quality. It is an instrument. She deploys the wide eyes, the small stumble, the tiny heartbroken sigh, with the precision of a duelist, and by the time her opponent realises the game was never innocent, the invitation has been withdrawn, the suitor rerouted, and Marigold is sitting in the warm spot. The Duke of Blackfriars, who has stared down the worst the pits ever offered, cannot refuse her anything and has stopped pretending otherwise.

She wears a ruby ribbon at her throat, a gift from His Grace, and her campaign to take the diamond of the season from Princess Lilac herself is the great sporting event of the present season. The Princess has the bloodline. Marigold has the barn. The wagering at Brindle's is even.

entities.title: Sweep of the Rookery
entities.content:
Sweep is black, wiry, and built out of whatever is left when a cat has burned away everything unnecessary. He is not of the ton and has told the ton so, in language the Society Papers declined to print. He was a sewer runner in the war against the Rat King, one of the cats who went down into the dark so that Mayfur could keep its ballrooms lit, and he came back up changed, with a torn ear, a permanent squint, and a settled conviction that trust is a luxury for cats who have never needed it.

What the ton persistently fails to understand about Sweep is that he made good. He owns, quietly and through intermediaries, half the fish stalls at Billingsgate and three chandleries besides. He could buy the gentlemen who cross the street to avoid him. He does not want their society; he wants their absence. And yet the strays of the Rookery eat every winter, and nobody can prove who pays for it, and Sweep has been heard to say that whoever it is must be a sentimental fool.

He extends something like courtesy to exactly two cats: the Dowager Countess of Nalewood, who was fair to him when fairness cost something, and the Duke of Blackfriars, with whom he shares a history from the pit years that neither of them has ever discussed. When the Dowager put his name forward for Almeow's, the ton called it madness. Sweep called it worse. The matter remains open.

entities.title: Marmalade Jack McTavish
entities.content:
Marmalade Jack is a very great deal of cat: big, ginger and white, with paws like dinner plates and a magnificent ringed tail that is, professionally speaking, his one liability, since it has been recognised leaving the scene of more than one of Mayfur's unsolved burglaries. He claims descent from a Highland clan of mousers and will tell you the whole lineage if you let him, most of it invented on the spot, all of it delivered with such warmth that cats have been known to applaud.

He is, beneath the charm, one of the most intelligent cats in Town, and it is exactly this that makes him so confounding to polite society. He can defeat any lock on Grimalkin Square, calculate odds at Brindle's to the third decimal, and quote poetry at length, yet he eats with the wrong fork, laughs at the opera in the sad parts, and once addressed the Dowager Countess of Nalewood as sweetheart. He survived it, which tells you most of what you need to know about his charm.

What the ton does not know is where the money goes. Jack lives simply for a successful thief. But his stepbrother, the Honourable Percival Grey, is delicate, and Dr. Valerian's bills are not, and Jack would sooner be hanged than let Percy learn what pays them. The theft of the Nalewood Collar has lately been laid at his door. The truth of that affair is stranger than the accusation.

entities.title: The Honourable Percival Grey
entities.content:
The Honourable Percival Grey, called Lamb by every lady in Mayfur, is a small grey cat of slight build with the most remarked-upon green eyes in Town, and a constitution that has never once cooperated with him. He is often ill, never complains, and possesses the particular gentleness of creatures who have decided that since the world will not spare them, they will spare the world instead. He is, by universal agreement, the sweetest soul in the ton, and the ladies of Mayfur compete for the privilege of looking after him with an intensity they otherwise reserve for the marriage mart.

Percy is a poet. His single slim volume, Songs of a Small Grey Cat, sold out its first printing within a fortnight, largely to purchasers who wanted to have been kind to him early. The poems, to everyone's surprise, are actually good: clear-eyed, unsentimental about illness, and very funny about ballrooms.

He worships his stepbrother, Marmalade Jack, whom he believes to be a successful dealer in Highland imports. He is the only cat in Mayfur who believes this. Whether Percy's innocence is perfect or simply a kindness he extends to Jack is a question Lady Whiskerdown has raised once and declined to pursue, on the grounds that some doors are better left shut by choice.

entities.title: Lady Whiskerdown, Authoress Unknown
entities.content:
Of Lady Whiskerdown, the ton knows precisely three things. First, that her Society Papers appear on doorsteps across Mayfur without any cat ever having been seen to deliver them. Second, that she is never wrong: names may be withheld, mercy may be extended, but no fact printed under her masthead has ever been overturned. Third, that she is one of them. The Papers know which fork Lord Fluffington used, what the Dowager said in a closed carriage, and how the wagering stood at Brindle's before the book was even balanced. Whoever she is, she was in the room.

Everything else is speculation, and Mayfur speculates at volume. The candidates have included Madame Sphynx, who hears everything on Ribbon Row; Mr. Pounce of Almeow's, who admits everyone and forgets no one; the Princess Lilac, on the theory that the voice matches; and the Dowager Countess of Nalewood herself, a theory the Dowager encourages because she finds it amusing.

Lady Whiskerdown has addressed the question exactly once, in her twelfth number: The ton asks who I am. The ton would do better to ask why it tells me everything. This authoress keeps her own counsel, and her own archive, and the archive is long.

entities.title: Lord Fluffington
entities.content:
Lord Fluffington is a Persian of immense coat and modest everything else. The coat is genuinely extraordinary: a silver cascade that requires, by his own valet's testimony, two hours of attention each morning and is insured, it is said, for more than his house. His conversation consists chiefly of the coat, his pedigree (fourteen generations, he will tell you, unprompted), and his opinion of draughts, which is low.

He entered the season of the comet as its most eligible bachelor and left it as its cautionary tale. It was Lady Whiskerdown who revealed, in her ninth number, that his lordship had come to a private understanding with Miss Henrietta Longwhisker and with Miss Beatrice Bobtail in the same fortnight, each lady under the impression she was the only one. The ton has a word for this. Lady Whiskerdown used it.

The affair ruined his marriage prospects for a season and made Mr. Bobtail his enemy for life, but the deeper wound was to his dignity, because ever since, the ton has been asking a second question, quieter and crueller than the first: how does a cat who does nothing all day keep a coat like that? Lady Whiskerdown has hinted, twice now, that the answer would astonish. His lordship has begun crossing the street to avoid printers.

entities.title: The Duchess of Fluffington
entities.content:
The Duchess of Fluffington is what her son would be if the coat came with a spine. A white Persian of the old school, she ran three seasons as the ton's most feared hostess before the Dowager Countess of Nalewood outlasted her, a defeat she has never acknowledged and never forgotten. Her at-homes remain the second-most important invitations in Mayfur, and she reminds cats of the ranking, gently, in every sentence.

The affair of her son's double courtship struck her, by all accounts, harder than it struck him. She retired from Town for a month, and returned with a single fixed purpose: to discover who leaked the matter to Lady Whiskerdown. Her theory changes weekly. She has accused the Longwhisker household, the Bobtail household, two lady's maids, a footcat, and, in one memorable outburst at Almeow's, the orchestra. The one possibility she has never entertained is the one the Rookery whispers: that the leak came from inside her own house.

She keeps a portrait of her son painted before the scandal and refers to it, rather than to him, when discussing the family's prospects.

entities.title: Miss Henrietta Longwhisker
entities.content:
Miss Henrietta Longwhisker is a sleek brown Havana of good family and better sense, which makes it all the stranger that she was the first of Lord Fluffington's two secret understandings. Her friends say she was not deceived by the coat but by the loneliness under it, which speaks well of her heart and poorly of her judgment.

When the ninth number of the Society Papers broke the affair, Miss Longwhisker did the thing nobody expected: she laughed. Publicly, at Almeow's, on the evening the number appeared, a clear ringing laugh that witnesses describe as the sound of a cage opening. She then crossed the room to Miss Beatrice Bobtail, the rival she had never known she had, and the two ladies have been inseparable allies ever since, a friendship the ton finds far more alarming than the scandal that produced it.

She has declined four offers since. She is reported to have said that she is holding out for a cat with less coat and more character, and that she is in no hurry, as the supply of the latter appears limited.

entities.title: Miss Beatrice Bobtail
entities.content:
Miss Beatrice Bobtail of Manxfield is a tidy tortoiseshell with the family's signature absence of tail and a temper the family signature does nothing to shorten. The Bobtails lost their tails generations ago and say nothing whatever about it; the ton has learned, at cost, to follow their example.

She was the second of Lord Fluffington's secret understandings, and unlike Miss Longwhisker she did not laugh when the news broke. She went home, took up her father's old dueling gloves, and had to be talked out of the rest by her mother over the course of a long evening. The talking-out was only partly successful: at the Fluffington at-home a week later, Miss Bobtail curtseyed to his lordship with perfect correctness and then complimented his coat so precisely, seam by seam, that witnesses swear he understood she knew something, though nobody could say what.

Her alliance with Miss Longwhisker is now the fixed social fact of the season. The two ladies attend everything together, decline suitors in committee, and are believed, by cats who watch such things, to be conducting a private investigation of their own into the matter of the Fluffington coat.

entities.title: Mr. Bobtail of Manxfield
entities.content:
Mr. Bobtail is the patriarch of Manxfield: a square, tail-less, iron-grey Manx who made the family fortune in herring and has never pretended otherwise. The ton's older houses look down on herring money. Mr. Bobtail looks down on cats who have never worked a morning tide, and as he can buy and sell most of them, the contempt has settled into a comfortable equilibrium.

The Fluffington affair turned him, overnight, from an amiable outsider into the most dangerous enemy in Town, because Mr. Bobtail does not fight with cuts and whispers. He fights with ledgers. In the season since, three of Lord Fluffington's creditors have quietly sold their notes, and all three notes now rest, the Rookery says, in a strongbox in Manxfield. What he intends to do with them is the subject of much wagering at Brindle's. Mr. Bobtail, asked directly, said only that herring teaches patience.

He dotes on his daughter Beatrice, funds her alliance with Miss Longwhisker without asking questions, and has standing instructions with his household that Lady Whiskerdown's Papers be ironed and presented before breakfast, as he regards the authoress as the one member of the ton who does honest work.

entities.title: Dr. Valerian, Physician
entities.content:
Dr. Valerian is Mayfur's most fashionable physician, a neat silver tabby with gold spectacles and a bedside manner so soothing that patients have been known to recover simply to please him. His name is a standing joke he pretends to be tired of and privately adores: valerian root being to cats what laudanum is to lesser species, the ton says the Doctor was named for his effect.

He is competent, which in Mayfur medicine makes him nearly unique, and discreet, which makes him invaluable. He attends the Dowager's headaches, the Duchess of Fluffington's nerves, and half the ton's discreet indispositions, and has never once been the source of a Whiskerdown item, a record both he and, curiously, the authoress herself appear to take pride in.

His most constant patient is the Honourable Percival Grey, whose fragile constitution he has managed for years with genuine tenderness. The bills are heavy. They are also, he has noticed, always paid, promptly, in coin, by a large ginger gentleman who waits in the mews and never gives a name. Dr. Valerian is a discreet cat. He has drawn his conclusions and keeps them in the same cabinet as everything else.

entities.title: Madame Sphynx, Modiste of Ribbon Row
entities.content:
Madame Sphynx is the finest dressmaker in Town and the only cat in Mayfur who genuinely needs her own merchandise. Hairless, elegant, and warm to the touch in a way her clients find either charming or unsettling, she arrived from the Continent a decade ago with two needles and an accent, and now dresses everyone worth dressing. Her atelier on Ribbon Row is where the ton goes to be fitted, and, not incidentally, to talk.

They talk because Madame is a professional listener. A fitting takes an hour; a cat cannot hold both a secret and a pose that long; and Madame's needle never pauses, which the ladies somehow take as proof she is not listening. She hears the engagements before the fathers do, the quarrels before the reconciliations, and the ruinations, always, before the ruined.

She is a perennial candidate for Lady Whiskerdown, a theory she deflects with the same answer every season: that if she printed what she heard, she would have no clients, and if she had no clients, she would hear nothing, and what kind of fool dismantles her own loom. The ton finds this reasoning airtight. Lady Whiskerdown, in her twenty-second number, called it the most sensible thing said in Mayfur that year, which either settles the question or does not.

entities.title: Mr. Pounce, Master of Ceremonies at Almeow's
entities.content:
Mr. Pounce has stood at the door of Almeow's Assembly Rooms for eleven seasons, a compact black-and-tan gentleman of perfect posture and total recall. He admits, announces, and, when required, declines, and it is the declining that has made him a power: a cat turned away by Mr. Pounce does not argue, because Mr. Pounce is never wrong about the list, and the list is never wrong about the ton.

He remembers every entrance ever made under his eye: who arrived with whom, who left early and why they said they were leaving, which couples came in separately and departed in the same carriage. He has never sold a memory. He regards the door of Almeow's as a kind of chapel and himself as its verger, and his discretion is so absolute that the ton has stopped testing it.

This has not stopped Lady Whiskerdown's readers from noticing that the Society Papers know a suspicious amount about the traffic through that door. Mr. Pounce, confronted with the theory that he is the authoress, permitted himself his only recorded joke: that he could not possibly be, as the Papers occasionally contain an error of precedence, and he would rather die. The vouchers question, and the matter of Sweep's candidacy, has lately made his chapel a battlefield, which grieves him.

entities.title: La Gattina, Soprano
entities.content:
La Gattina is the reigning voice of the Theatre Royal, a dramatic tortoiseshell from the southern peninsula whose upper register has cracked two chandelier pendants and one engagement. She performs rarely, cancels often, and is adored in exact proportion to her unreliability, the ton having long ago decided that a diva who always appears is merely an employee.

Her feud with Princess Lilac is the second-best entertainment in Town. It began at a musicale where the Princess, asked her opinion of the aria, replied that in Siam such a sound would be answered by the palace guard. La Gattina responded from the stage, in translated verse, at the next three performances. Honours are considered even, and hostesses now take care never to invite both, or, if the season is dull, to invite both.

Off the stage she is shrewd, generous, and unexpectedly kind to the chorus, whose members she feeds and defends like a fierce aunt. She was among the first subscribers to the benefit for Mr. Grey, and sang at it without fee, an evening cats still describe to those who missed it with a certain quiet cruelty.

entities.title: One-Ear Otto
entities.content:
One-Ear Otto runs the night side of the Rookery: the card cellars, the fence yards, and a share of the catmint trade he pretends is smaller than it is. A heavy brindled tom with the ear he is named for and a smile cats trust exactly as far as it extends, Otto served in the sewer campaign alongside Sweep, and the two came up out of the dark with the same nightmares and opposite conclusions. Sweep decided never to owe anyone anything. Otto decided everyone should owe him.

Their cold war divides the Rookery street by street. Otto's crews do not touch Sweep's stalls; Sweep's chandleries do not light Otto's cellars; and when the two meet, which the Rookery arranges to happen rarely, they speak with the terrible politeness of cats who once carried each other through the dark and can never forgive the weight.

Otto's ambition has lately turned upward. The catmint reaching Mayfur's ballrooms moves, the whisper goes, on his account, and a gentleman with debts and a famous coat is said to be among his customers. Lady Whiskerdown is known to be pulling this thread. Otto is known to know she is pulling it.

entities.title: The Beldam of the Rookery
entities.content:
Nobody remembers the Beldam young, which is how she prefers it. A grey-muzzled, yellow-eyed matriarch of indeterminate breed and unlimited memory, she keeps a den at the heart of the Rookery where the mint is weighed, the disputes are settled, and the real history of Town is stored, the history that never reaches the Society Papers because it would burn them.

She grew the first catmint garden in the Rookery in the hungry years after the war, when the veterans came home to nothing and needed somewhere soft to put the dark. She will tell you, if she decides you are worth telling, that she is not proud of what the trade became, and that pride is a Mayfur luxury anyway. Otto runs the trade now, and pays her the courtesies. Everyone pays the Beldam the courtesies.

She knew Sweep as a half-starved kitten and fed him before he learned to distrust food with a price on it; hers never had one, and he has never forgotten it. She is one of perhaps three cats living who know the truth of what happened between Sweep and the young fighter who became the Duke of Blackfriars, and she has kept it for twenty years, on the grounds that some stories are load-bearing.

entities.title: Mr. Tomlin of the Town Tabby
entities.content:
Mr. Tomlin publishes the Town Tabby, Mayfur's second society paper, a distinction with the same relation to the first as the second cat through a door. An eager orange tom with ink-stained cuffs and a genius for arriving just after the story, Tomlin has spent four seasons trying to beat Lady Whiskerdown to a single item and has succeeded once, on the subject of a garden party's seating plan, an exclusive he has referenced in print eleven times since.

His method is industry where hers is access: he attends everything, interviews everyone, and pays footcats for scraps. The result is a paper that is frequently first with the facts nobody wanted and reliably second with the ones they did. The ton reads him anyway, partly for the sport of it, and partly because his errors are themselves informative, being a reliable map of what his sources want believed.

His obsession with unmasking Lady Whiskerdown is total and public. He has printed seven theories, retracted six, and maintains a wall of string and clippings his housekeeper describes as the saddest thing she has ever dusted. Lady Whiskerdown has mentioned him once, kindly, which he is aware was worse than cruelty.

entities.title: Captain Bootes, R.N.
entities.content:
Captain Bootes of the Royal Navy is the ton's approved kind of hero: a tall black tom with four white feet, a pleasant scar, and a uniform that does half his conversation for him. He commanded a fisheries frigate in the war against the Rat King, held the Billingsgate approaches through the worst winter of the blockade, and came home to find himself famous, which he has borne with a good grace that only occasionally slips.

It slips on the subject of the sewer campaign. The Captain is welcome everywhere and knows it; the cats who fought below the streets are welcome nowhere and he knows that too. He has said, at Brindle's, loudly enough to be intended for the whole room, that the war was won in the dark by cats this club would not admit to its kitchen, and that he drinks their health whether or not the company joins him. The company, these days, mostly joins him. It is harder to snub a toast than a cat.

He is unmarried, hunted accordingly, and entirely oblivious to the campaign Miss Marigold's rivals believe she is running in his direction. His affections, the better observers say, point somewhere less convenient: he has danced with Miss Henrietta Longwhisker three times this season, and the Captain does not do things in threes by accident.

entities.title: The Reverend Mr. Mouser
entities.content:
The Reverend Mr. Mouser holds the living of St. Gertrude's-in-the-Square and the unofficial chaplaincy of the entire ton, a flock he describes, from the pulpit and with affection, as the most beautifully dressed sinners in the kingdom. A round, comfortable, grey-and-white gentleman with a bell-clear voice, he preaches short sermons on long vices and is therefore universally beloved.

He is a fixture at every wedding, christening, and deathbed in Mayfur, and this circuit has made him, quite against his intentions, one of the best-informed cats in Town. Unlike Madame Sphynx he cannot be theorised into the Whiskerdown question, because his one public feud is with the Society Papers themselves: he preaches against them twice a season, on the text of the unbridled tongue, and is understood to read every number the morning it appears, for professional reasons.

His quiet work is in the Rookery, where he keeps a second, shabbier chapel and asks no questions of the cats who shelter there. He buried the sewer campaign's dead when no Mayfur church would take them, and the Rookery, which forgets nothing, has decided he is permanent.

entities.title: Young Lord Frisk
entities.content:
Lord Frisk is nineteen, wealthy, and a danger chiefly to himself. A lanky cream-coloured heir with more energy than any single body should be asked to contain, he has in one season overturned a punt on the Saucerine, been banned from the Theatre Royal's chandelier gallery, and, most famously, chased the carriage of the Ambassador from the Kingdom of Dogs the full length of Grimalkin Square before the enormity of the thing caught up with him, somewhere around the fountain.

The diplomatic incident took a week to smooth over. The Ambassador, to his lasting credit, found it hilarious, and has since taken a benevolent interest in the boy, inviting him to the embassy and introducing him, with visible mischief, as my young pursuer. The ton was less amused; the Dowager Countess of Nalewood rapped his ankles in full view of Almeow's, an honour that has, perversely, made him.

Under the chaos there is, the hopeful note, a decent heart. He was among the first to subscribe to the benefit for Mr. Grey, for a sum that made his guardian sit down, and when asked why, said simply that Mr. Grey had once been kind to him at a party where nobody else was.

entities.title: His Excellency the Ambassador from the Kingdom of Dogs
entities.content:
His Excellency is a pug of impeccable manners and no discretion whatsoever, which makes him simultaneously the most correct and the most dangerous guest in Mayfur. Posted to Town three years ago to maintain the long peace between the kingdoms, he has succeeded so thoroughly that the ton now forgets, for whole evenings at a time, that he is a dog, remembering only when he laughs, which is often, and at volume.

His diplomatic method is simple: he tells everyone everything. Secrets, he has explained, are a form of hoarding, and hoarding is bad for the digestion. This policy has caused four scandals, averted two duels, and made him the most reliably quoted source in the Society Papers, where he appears as a certain foreign gentleman of candid habits. He is perfectly aware of the epithet and has asked, through channels, whether he might have it engraved.

He keeps a standing table at the Theatre Royal, adores La Gattina to the point of learned commentary, and has adopted young Lord Frisk, his onetime pursuer, as a kind of protege in chaos. The peace, under his stewardship, has never been warmer or louder.

entities.title: The Rat King
entities.content:
The Rat King was the great enemy of the last generation, and the reason the present one dances so hard. Historians dispute whether he was one rat, a dynasty, or a title passed down the tunnels, but the horde he raised was real enough: it took the granaries at Longmarsh, closed the river for a season, and pressed as far as the Billingsgate approaches before the fleet and the winter broke him.

The war that bears his name lasted four years and drew in every kind of cat: the fleet toms in their frigates, the yard militias, and, at the end, the sewer runners, volunteers who went into the tunnels themselves to find and finish the King in his own dark. What happened below the streets was never fully told. The runners who came back did not talk, the crown did not ask, and the ton, once the bunting came down, found the whole subject dampening.

He is officially dead. The Rookery, which fought him closest, is not officially anything, and old runners are known to leave a corner of their plate untouched, a habit nobody explains to outsiders. His memory does quiet work in Town to this day: it is the wall every argument about the Rookery finally backs into, the unpaid bill under the ballroom floor.

entities.title: House Blackfriars
entities.content:
House Blackfriars is the strangest of the great houses because it is also the newest, and the ton can never quite decide which fact to hold against it. The dukedom is three generations old, won, the polite version goes, in service to the crown during the disorders; the impolite version, whispered and never printed, involves the pits, a wager, and a title no one else would take. The present Duke has made the house what it is: the place disputes go to die, the closest thing Mayfur has to a court of appeal.

The house colours are black and white, worn without ornament. The household is small for its rank and ferociously loyal: the Duke pays above the going rate, promotes from the Rookery without comment, and has dismissed exactly one servant in his tenure, for unkindness to a kitchen kitten.

Its weaknesses are the family. Lady Tabitha generates a scandal a season; Miss Marigold, the ward, is conducting a social campaign of ambitions nobody has measured yet; and the Duke himself carries a history that at least three cats in Town could sell, if they dared. The house's unofficial motto, attributed to the Duke and denied by him, is said to be: fair first, gentle second, and after that, God help you.

entities.title: House Nalewood
entities.content:
House Nalewood is old the way rivers are old: it was here before the map, and the map was drawn around it. The earldom predates Almeow's, predates the war, predates, the family likes to imply, most of the alphabet. Its fortunes have thinned over the centuries, and its present establishment is modest by great-house standards, but nobody measures Nalewood in silver. Its currency is the Dowager.

The Dowager Countess has outlived the male line's vigour; the present earl, her grandnephew, lives contentedly in the country with his mice and his correspondence, and Town affairs are hers entirely. Under her hand the house has become something no other house is: neutral ground. Feuding families meet in her drawing room because refusing her invitation is unthinkable and misbehaving under her roof is worse.

The house's treasure is the Nalewood Collar, three centuries of history in worked silver and river pearls, worn once a season at the opening ball. Its theft this spring, and the strange manner of its return, remains the ton's most carefully unexamined subject, because the Dowager has let it be known that she considers the matter closed, and what the Dowager considers closed, stays closed.

entities.title: House Fluffington
entities.content:
House Fluffington built its name on coat. For six generations the family has bred for silver, length, and lustre, and the results hang in the portrait hall like weather: banks of magnificent fur with, increasingly, less and less cat underneath. The house's fortunes were made in fine goods, combs, brushes, and the famous Fluffington pomade, a trade origin the family has spent two generations trying to perfume away.

The Duchess keeps the standard up; her son has let it down twice over, first in the matter of the double courtship, and second in the quieter, still-unfolding matter of the debts. The house's finances are the Rookery's favourite riddle: the establishment is grand, the entertainments lavish, the pomade concern sold years ago, and the arithmetic, cats who can count observe, does not arrive anywhere respectable.

Mr. Bobtail of Manxfield is buying the family's paper note by note, for purposes he declines to explain. The Duchess does not know. Lord Fluffington, it is increasingly suspected, does, and the strain of knowing is visible at his collar, where even the coat has begun, faintly, to dull.

entities.title: The Bobtails of Manxfield
entities.content:
The Bobtails of Manxfield lost their tails generations ago and say nothing whatever about it, a policy so total that new acquaintances are warned by third parties, in advance, in writing. What the family says a great deal about is herring, honest work, and the precise weight of every favour ever done them, a ledger kept in Mr. Bobtail's head to the farthing.

They are new to Mayfur as the ton counts newness, forty years, and their money still smells faintly of the morning tide to noses that choose to notice. Fewer noses choose to, these days. The family's fortune has passed the point where it can be condescended to safely, and Mr. Bobtail's response to the Fluffington affair has taught Town a second lesson: the Bobtails do not forgive, they foreclose.

The house's rising asset is Miss Beatrice, whose alliance with Miss Longwhisker has given the family its first genuine foothold in the ton's inner rooms. Her father watches the campaign with the quiet pride of a cat who spent forty years buying the ticket and has finally seen the play begin.

entities.title: House Longwhisker
entities.content:
House Longwhisker is what the ton means when it says a good family: old enough, rich enough, and sensible enough never to be interesting, a record of four unbroken generations that Miss Henrietta has now cheerfully ended. The family seat is in the eastern counties; the Town establishment is comfortable; and the Longwhisker whiskers are, as advertised, remarkable, the longest reliably recorded in the kingdom, a point of quiet vanity in a family otherwise armoured against the sin.

The family's response to the Fluffington affair was characteristic: no scenes, no statements, and a sudden, total closure of every door Lord Fluffington had ever walked through. Longwhisker influence is like their whiskers, fine, long, and felt before it is seen; his lordship discovered over one winter that his invitations had simply stopped, everywhere east of the Square, without anyone appearing to have done anything.

Miss Henrietta's new alliance with the Bobtail girl has the family's full, faintly bemused support. Her father is reported to have said that he spent twenty years teaching her caution and is delighted to learn it did not take.

entities.title: The Greys of Lower Gnawbury
entities.content:
The Greys of Lower Gnawbury are the ton's favourite kind of tragedy: an honourable name attached to no money whatsoever. The barony is real, the manners are exquisite, and the roof of the Gnawbury house has been, for some years, a matter of faith. The late Lord Grey married twice; the first marriage produced the Honourable Percival, the second brought a stepson into the family, a large ginger boy from a Highland line nobody could quite trace, and then his lordship died leaving both boys the name, the manners, and the roof.

What the family lives on is the standing puzzle of Mayfur. Percy's poems sell, but poetry has never yet paid a physician. Jack deals, he says, in Highland imports, and the imports must do well, because the bills are met, the house is warm, and Percy wants for nothing. The ton has decided not to look at this closely, partly from delicacy and partly because everyone is fond of Percy and most cats, despite themselves, are fond of Jack.

The brothers' devotion to each other is the house's whole estate, and the ton, which is not sentimental about much, is sentimental about that.

entities.title: The Rookery Cats
entities.content:
The Rookery cats are not a house and would bite you for suggesting it, but the ton files them as one because the ton has no other drawer for a power it cannot invite to dinner. They are the porters, the fence-keepers, the fish-stall crews, the mint-growers, the survivors of the sewer campaign and the descendants of every cat Mayfur ever pushed east of the wall, and they hold together by a web of debts, courtesies, and remembered kindnesses more binding than any pedigree.

Their governance is informal and absolute. The Beldam keeps the memory, Otto runs the night trades, Sweep anchors the honest ones, and disputes that cannot be settled among those three go, by a very old arrangement nobody will explain, across the river to the Duke of Blackfriars.

Mayfur needs them and dislikes knowing it. Every fish on every table crossed a Rookery paw; every ballroom's candles came off a Rookery cart; and, since the war, every cat in Town owes them a debt that was never toasted. The Dowager's sponsorship of Sweep at Almeow's is the first attempt in a generation to acknowledge any of this out loud, and both sides of the wall are watching it like weather.

entities.title: The Siamese Delegation
entities.content:
The Siamese Delegation occupies the tall house at the north end of Grimalkin Square, flies a silk pennant no one in Town can read, and maintains, in the person of Princess Lilac and her small suite, the kingdom of Siam's only permanent presence in the west. What the delegation actually does is a favourite Mayfur riddle. It issues no papers, receives few callers, and appears to exist chiefly so that the Princess may decline invitations on its stationery.

The suite consists of four: an elderly major-domo of great dignity, two athletic cousins who exercise on the roof at dawn to the alarm of the neighbours, and a silent seal-point secretary who is, in the Rookery's professional opinion, the most dangerous cat on the Square. The delegation's dispatches go east twice a season by ship, and Mr. Tomlin of the Town Tabby once spent a month trying to learn what was in them, an episode the secretary is believed to have ended with a single visit and no words.

Why a princess of Siam has spent two seasons in Town is a question the Princess has answered differently at every dinner, each answer perfectly convincing at the time.

entities.title: Lady Whiskerdown's Society Papers
entities.content:
The Society Papers appear on Mayfur's doorsteps at irregular intervals, always before breakfast, always without a delivery cat ever having been seen, a logistical feat the ton has given up explaining and settled for enjoying. Each number is four pages, close-set, in a type the printers of Town swear belongs to none of their houses, on paper the stationers swear the same of.

The voice is the thing. Arch, precise, merciless with the deserving and unexpectedly gentle with the rest, the Papers do not merely report the ton, they grade it. A kind mention lifts a season; the withholding of a name is understood as mercy and remembered as debt; and the full treatment, name, dates, and that closing turn of phrase the readers call the flick of the tail, has ended two engagements, one card-ring, and the social career of the late Lord Bristlepate.

No fact printed in the Papers has ever been overturned. This is the true mystery, greater than the authoress's name: not who she is, but how she is always right. The Papers' own answer, printed once, is kept folded in more than one Mayfur desk: I am not clever, gentle reader. I merely remember what you tell me, which is everything.

entities.title: The Nalewood Collar
entities.content:
The Nalewood Collar is three centuries of the family's history in worked silver and river pearls: seventeen pearls, one for each countess who has worn it, the newest added at each succession and the oldest gone cloudy as a winter window. It is heavy, slightly cruel to wear, and completely magnificent, and the Dowager wears it exactly once a season, at the opening ball at Almeow's, where its arrival is the true beginning of the year.

Its theft this spring, from a locked case in a locked room in a house that has never been robbed, stopped Town like a thrown shoe. Suspicion travelled where suspicion travels: a ringed tail had been seen in the mews, and the wagers at Brindle's made Marmalade Jack the thief by supper. What no wager anticipated was the return. Eleven days later the collar was back in its case, the case locked, the room locked, and laid beside it a single sprig of dried heather, which is, cats who know the Highlands say, an apology.

The Dowager declined to pursue the matter and has forbidden its discussion, publicly. Privately, guests swear she wears the collar now with a small extra satisfaction, as if it had been somewhere interesting and told her about it.

entities.title: Miss Marigold's Ruby Ribbon
entities.content:
The ribbon is red silk, unremarkable in itself, and Miss Marigold is never seen without it. The Duke of Blackfriars gave it to her the week she arrived from Foldingworth Farm, reportedly because she had admired, with enormous eyes and a very small voice, a ribbon in a shop window on Ribbon Row that turned out to cost rather less than the Duke assumed anything could cost, a discovery that is said to have troubled him for days.

The ton, which reads dress the way scholars read manuscripts, has assigned the ribbon a meaning far above its price: it is the visible sign of Blackfriars protection, and cats calculating the risks of crossing Miss Marigold are understood to be calculating, really, about the ribbon. Madame Sphynx, who knows exactly what the silk cost, has been heard to observe that it is the most expensive object in Mayfur.

Marigold herself maintains it is simply pretty. She has, however, worn it in a different knot on three notable occasions, each followed within the week by a social reversal for somebody, and the ladies who track such things now report on the knot the way sailors report weather.

entities.title: The Fluffington Coat
entities.content:
Lord Fluffington's coat is the most admired object in Mayfur and, lately, the most examined. A silver cascade of impossible length and lustre, it is groomed two hours daily, insured beyond the house that shelters it, and maintained, this is the delicate part, at a cost the family's visible income has not explained for at least two years.

The question of the coat began as a joke at Brindle's and has curdled into something with teeth. The pomade concern is sold; the rents are mortgaged; Mr. Bobtail holds the paper; and still the coat gleams, groomed by a specialist who comes at dawn and is paid, the mews says, in coin. Lady Whiskerdown has twice printed the phrase borrowed plumage in adjacent paragraphs, which in her grammar is not an accident.

The Rookery's theory is the simplest and the worst: that the coat is financed the way desperate things are financed east of the wall, and that a certain brindled gentleman with one ear holds more Fluffington paper than even Mr. Bobtail knows. If that is true, then the most beautiful object in Mayfur is collateral, and the season it comes due will be one for the archive.

entities.title: Songs of a Small Grey Cat
entities.content:
Songs of a Small Grey Cat is a slim volume of thirty-one poems by the Honourable Percival Grey, published by subscription last winter and sold out within a fortnight. The first purchasers, it must be honestly said, were buying kindness: Percy is beloved, Percy is frail, and owning his little book was that season's way of having been good to him early.

Then cats read it. The poems are not what anyone expected from the gentlest invalid in Mayfur. They are clear-eyed and dry: a poem about fever that never mentions fear and is entirely about the pattern of light on a counterpane; a ballroom poem, much quoted, that observes the dancers the way a naturalist observes wading birds; and the sequence everyone pretends not to cry at, seven short verses addressed to an unnamed brother who goes out at night, and what it costs to pretend not to notice, and how pretending can itself be a kind of gift.

The second printing sold to cats who wanted the poems. The third is subscribed already. Jack carries a first edition everywhere, so worn at one particular page that booksellers could tell you, if they dared, exactly which seven verses it opens to.

entities.title: The Friar's Placard
entities.content:
In the pit years, fights in the Rookery were announced by hand-lettered placards nailed to the wall of the old brewery, and collectors of low history prize them the way Mayfur prizes miniatures. One placard above all: THE FRIAR, in smoke-blacked capitals, against a challenger whose name has been torn away, dated the last night of the pits' great era. It is the only surviving placard bearing the Friar's name. Every other was burned, systematically, by parties unknown, in the month before a certain black-and-white tom was gazetted Duke of Blackfriars.

The surviving placard belongs to the Beldam of the Rookery, who keeps it face-down under the mint scales and produces it, perhaps once a decade, for visitors she wishes to unsettle. The torn corner is the point of it. Who the challenger was that night, and what happened in that ring, and why the Friar never fought again, are questions the placard raises and the Beldam declines, pleasantly, to answer.

She has said only this, and only once: that two cats went into that ring, and neither of them lost, which was the whole trouble.

entities.title: Mayfur
entities.content:
Mayfur is the fashionable quarter of Town: the squares, the tall houses, the shops of Ribbon Row, and the several hundred cats who constitute, in their own firm opinion, everyone. Its boundaries are nowhere written and universally known, running from the river walk in the south to the old wall in the east, beyond which lies the Rookery and about which Mayfur prefers not to think at dinner.

The quarter lives by the season: the ton assembles in spring when the sunning walls warm, conducts its courtships, feuds, and ruinations through the summer, and scatters to the country when the first fogs come off the river. The rhythm is fixed, the cast rotates, and the whole performance is recorded, graded, and occasionally redirected by Lady Whiskerdown's Society Papers, which Mayfur affects to deplore and reads to the last line.

Its great institutions are Almeow's for assembly, Brindle's for wagering, the Theatre Royal for spectacle, and St. Gertrude's for repentance, conveniently arranged, as the Reverend Mr. Mouser observes, in the order cats generally require them.

entities.title: Grimalkin Square
entities.content:
Grimalkin Square is the centre of Mayfur and therefore, its residents would say, of the world. Four terraces of tall houses face a private garden of old plane trees, a fountain stocked, by ancient subscription, with ornamental fish nobody is supposed to touch, and the long south-facing sunning wall where the ton takes its afternoons.

The addresses tell the whole social map: Blackfriars House holds the west side entire; the Dowager Countess of Nalewood keeps the oldest house on the north terrace, three doors from the silk pennant of the Siamese Delegation; and the Fluffington establishment commands the east, its window boxes replanted weekly at an expense the Rookery finds professionally interesting.

The Square's garden is nominally private and practically the ton's parliament. Matches are floated on its gravel walks, feuds are suspended under its planes by unwritten treaty, and the fountain's fish, it must be recorded, are touched constantly, a crime the Square's kittens are taught by their own parents with the solemnity of an inheritance. Lord Frisk's pursuit of the Ambassador's carriage ran the full length of the north walk, and the gravel, old residents insist, has never quite settled since.

entities.title: Almeow's Assembly Rooms
entities.content:
Almeow's is the ton's holy of holies: the assembly rooms in King Street whose Wednesday balls are the season's fixed stars and whose vouchers are the true currency of Mayfur, rarer than gold and less arguable. The rooms themselves are handsome rather than grand, a long ballroom with the famous high mantel, a card room, and a supper room serving refreshments so austere that their badness is part of the mystique; one does not go to Almeow's to eat.

One goes to exist. Admission is governed by the patronesses, seven ladies of terrifying accumulated consequence, and executed at the door by Mr. Pounce, whose list is never wrong. To hold vouchers is to be inside the walls of the world; to lose them, and they can be lost in an evening, is social death with dancing after.

The high mantel deserves its own history: leaping to it uninvited is the classic folly of new money, and the roll of cats who have misjudged it is long and cherished. Princess Lilac holds the record, set in a single motion while conversing. The present crisis, over the Dowager's sponsorship of Sweep of the Rookery, is the gravest in the institution's history, and the patronesses are, for the first time anyone can remember, publicly divided.

entities.title: The Saucerine
entities.content:
The Saucerine is the ornamental water in the great park west of Mayfur: a long, shallow, silver curve, stocked with carp of great age and greater cunning, crossed by the arched bridge where the ton promenades at five and misbehaves at midnight. Its name is old and disputed; its function is not. By day it is the most respectable water in the kingdom. After dark it is where Mayfur goes to do the things Lady Whiskerdown writes about.

The carp are an institution in themselves. Generations of fashionable cats have crouched at the rail, measured the drop, and reflected on the proverb the park keepers post each spring: the fish are not worth the swim. Most heed it. Lady Tabitha of Blackfriars, famously, has not, twice, from railings she had been expressly told not to walk, and the carp of the Saucerine are now said to recognise her.

The midnight bridge has hosted duels, elopements, reconciliations, and, this season, the unexplained encounter between Lady Tabitha and a large ginger gentleman that the ton has been forbidden to discuss and therefore discusses at every table. The park keepers rake the gravel each dawn, erasing the night's evidence with the neutrality of long practice.

entities.title: Brindle's
entities.content:
Brindle's is the gentlemen's club of St. Jerome Street: deep chairs, old port, a cellar of legendary cheeses, and the wager book, which is the club's true purpose and the ton's actuarial record. Everything is wagered at Brindle's: matches, races, the date of the first fog, the identity of Lady Whiskerdown (a standing book, seven years open, odds revised weekly), and, this season, the diamond question, on which the book stands even and the sums stand alarming.

Membership is by election and blackball, and the club's politics are a shadow-play of the ton's. The Duke of Blackfriars belongs and rarely attends; Lord Fluffington attends and, the whisper goes, rarely settles; Mr. Bobtail was elected two years ago on the strength of his fortune and his silences, and has been quietly buying the room's respect the way he buys everything, at par and without haste.

The wager book's most famous page is ruled off in black and never explained to visitors: a bet from the pit years, terms coded, stakes blank, marked only settled in a hand the older members recognise and do not discuss. Club lore holds that on the night it was settled, two cats sat until dawn in the window seats, and the port went down by four bottles, and nothing was ever said.

entities.title: The Rookery
entities.content:
East of the old wall, the streets narrow, the washing lines take over the sky, and Town becomes the Rookery: a dense, loud, self-governing warren of yards, cellars, stalls, and stairs where most of the actual work of the city gets done and none of the credit arrives. Mayfur uses the name as a shudder. The Rookery uses it as an address, and corrects your pronunciation.

It is poor, and it is not simple. The fish trade, the candle trade, the porterage, the mint trade, and several trades with no daylight names all run through its yards; its own law, administered by the Beldam with Otto and Sweep as its estranged pillars, is faster and frequently fairer than the crown's; and its memory is the longest in Town. The Rookery remembers who fought in the sewers, who sold short weights in the hungry years, and which Mayfur houses paid their tradescats late, information that has a way of mattering decades on.

The war sits under everything here. The sewer campaign was mustered from these yards, and the cats who came back went unthanked into the same cold cellars they had left. Mayfur owes the Rookery its lights, its dinners, and its survival, and the Rookery keeps the account the way the Beldam keeps everything: patiently, in full, and with interest accruing.

entities.title: Billingsgate Fish Market
entities.content:
Billingsgate is where Town's appetite meets the river: the great fish market whose morning tide sets the day's prices and whose smell, Mayfur complains, sets everything else. The market opens in the dark, peaks at dawn, and is finished by the hour fashionable cats wake, which is why the two worlds can share a city while never once meeting on purpose.

The market's politics are Rookery politics. Sweep owns half the stalls through intermediaries and runs them straight: fair weights, honest ice, and a standing rule that the last hour's unsold catch goes east of the wall at cost. Mr. Bobtail's herring fortune began here forty years ago with one barrow and a temper, and he still walks the market twice a season, unannounced, to remind himself, he says, what money smells like before it learns manners.

In the war, Billingsgate was the prize: the Rat King's horde pressed to its very approaches before Captain Bootes' frigates and the blockade winter broke them. The market keeps the memory in its own way, with a brass plate at the river stairs listing no names, only a number, and the words THE TIDE HELD.

entities.title: Ribbon Row
entities.content:
Ribbon Row is Mayfur's street of shops: the milliners, the glovers, the stationers, the perfumers, and, at the good end, the atelier of Madame Sphynx, before whose fitting rooms the whole ton eventually passes and inside which it eventually talks. The Row is short, expensive, and perfectly informed; its shopkeepers know the season's engagements a week before the fathers and its failures a month before the creditors.

The Row's economy runs on credit and its society on the order book. To be dressed by Madame is standing; to be dressed by Madame on time is favour; and to be told, with infinite continental regret, that Madame is quite full this season, is a sentence from which reputations do not always recover.

It was in a Ribbon Row window that a certain red silk ribbon caught the eye of a newly arrived farm kitten, and the resulting purchase, by the Duke of Blackfriars, for a sum smaller than his usual tip, is the Row's favourite story about itself: proof, the shopkeepers say, that the street sells meaning, and the materials are incidental.

entities.title: The Theatre Royal
entities.content:
The Theatre Royal on Purring Lane is where the ton goes to watch and, more importantly, to be watched: five gilt tiers, a chandelier of dangerous magnificence, and sightlines engineered, the joke runs, so that every box can see every other box and nobody need see the stage at all. La Gattina rules the boards when she chooses to appear; the pit rules the verdicts; and the boxes conduct, above both, a season-long opera of their own with better plots.

The chandelier gallery, a catwalk in the honest sense, is officially closed to patrons and unofficially the finest vantage in Town, which is why young Lord Frisk was banned from it and why nobody believes the ban is holding. The Ambassador from the Kingdom of Dogs keeps the largest box and the loudest laugh, timed, connoisseurs note, with genuine theatrical instinct.

The benefit for Mr. Grey was held here on a wet Thursday in April, and cats who were present speak of it the way veterans speak of weather: the house full to the gallery, La Gattina unpaid and in voice, and a small grey cat in the front box being looked after, for one evening, by the entire world at once.

entities.title: Foldingworth Farm
entities.content:
Foldingworth Farm lies two days' travel from Town in the soft hills of the western counties: a dairy farm of no distinction whatever except the one it will carry forever, as the birthplace of Miss Marigold, ward of the Duke of Blackfriars. The farm cats of Foldingworth are a numerous, capable, unsentimental tribe who hunt the barns, run the dairy's margins, and regard their famous daughter's career in Town with a pride so dry it could be mistaken for indifference.

Marigold was born in the great barn, third of six, in a litter her mother describes as five good workers and one project. The warm spot by the dairy door, the throne of Foldingworth society and the first prize Marigold ever took, is now pointed out to visitors, of whom there are, to the farm's mystification, beginning to be some.

The Duke found her there on a shooting visit, or, as the farm tells it, she found him: a half-grown calico fluff who walked out of the barn, examined the largest and most dangerous cat in the kingdom for a long moment, and climbed him like a tree. The Duke's party left two days later with one additional passenger and no explanation his friends ever received.

entities.title: The Sunning Wall
entities.content:
The Sunning Wall is the long south-facing wall of Grimalkin Square's garden, and from March to October it is the most fiercely contested real estate in the kingdom. The wall takes the sun from mid-morning to early evening; its warmth is graded by the yard, with the stretch above the espaliered pear universally acknowledged the finest; and its unwritten seating precedence is more exactly observed than anything at court.

The precedence is this: the Dowager Countess of Nalewood holds the pear stretch by right so ancient nobody can name its origin, and holds it whether or not she is present, cats having been known to sit a careful yard short of an empty space for entire afternoons. Below her, rank, age, and the season's standing sort themselves in a silent daily negotiation that visitors find eerie and residents find restful.

The wall is where the ton actually happens. Matches are made there at two in the afternoon that ballrooms only ratify at midnight; the Papers' sharpest items are traceable, the observant note, to conversations held drowsily along its warm brick; and the one law binding all ranks alike is the wall's own: no cat, whatever the provocation, is ever to be pushed off.

entities.title: St. Gertrude's-in-the-Square
entities.content:
St. Gertrude's-in-the-Square is Mayfur's parish church, named for the patroness of cats and travellers, and serves the ton's spiritual needs at the fashionable hour of eleven, by which time, the Reverend Mr. Mouser observes, most of his congregation has already committed everything they intend to confess. The church is small, honey-stoned, and lovely, with a memorial window to the war dead that names the fleet, the militias, and, after a quiet campaign by the Reverend that took him four years, the sewer runners, in letters the same size as everyone else's.

The Reverend keeps a second chapel east of the wall and shuttles between his two flocks with a lack of visible effort that is itself a sermon. St. Gertrude's registers hold the ton's whole private history, marriages, births, and burials, and the Reverend guards them like a dragon, having refused, on the record, to open them even for the Dowager, an act of courage still discussed in awed tones on the sunning wall.

entities.title: Manxfield
entities.content:
Manxfield is the Bobtail establishment on the unfashionable but rising side of the park: a big, square, comfortable house that Mayfur called a warehouse with windows when it was built and has since learned to call handsome, the family's fortune having grown to the size where taste follows it around. The house is run with mercantile precision, entertains rarely and well, and keeps, in Mr. Bobtail's study, the famous strongbox whose contents, three notes of Fluffington debt and rising, are the subject of more speculation than most marriages.

The name came with the family from the island, and the house observes island customs Mayfur finds obscure: a lamp kept lit over the door for cats caught out by weather, a standing table for any sailor of the old fleet, and the total, absolute, never-explained silence on the subject of tails.

entities.title: Lower Gnawbury
entities.content:
