Lower Gnawbury is genteel poverty's home address: a short terrace of once-fine houses on Mayfur's fraying southern edge, where good names go when the money has gone first. The residents keep standards with a discipline the rich never need: brass polished, steps whitened, cards left, and the universal fiction maintained that everyone is merely between fortunes.

Number four is the Grey house, warm against all arithmetic, its small parlour the terrace's one genuine salon. Percy receives there on his good days, propped and shining, and half of fashionable Mayfur has learned the way south, the ladies bringing calf's-foot jelly and taking away, they report, more comfort than they carried in. The terrace has adopted him collectively; his good days are announced door to door by the milk cat, and on his bad ones the whole street, by unspoken arrangement, goes quietly.

entities.title: The Longmarsh Granaries
entities.content:
The Longmarsh granaries stand where the river widens east of Town: the kingdom's larder, rank upon rank of timber stores that hold the harvest between the country and the city's plate. Their fall to the Rat King's horde in the second year of the war was the conflict's darkest hour; Town went hungry that winter, and cats of a certain age still will not waste bread.

The granaries were retaken in the campaign that made the fleet's name and broke the horde's advance, and they have been rebuilt in stone and iron, patrolled now by a hereditary corps of granary cats who hold their commissions, uniquely, from the crown itself. The Longmarsh corps recruits without regard to quarter, and it is one of the few services where a Rookery kitten and a Mayfur younger son wear the same coat and answer the same bell, a fact the Reverend Mr. Mouser has preached on more than once.

entities.title: The War Against the Rat King
entities.content:
The war began, as the histories now agree, with the granaries: the Rat King's horde took Longmarsh in a single autumn night, and Town woke to learn that its larder belonged to the enemy. Four years followed that divided every life in the kingdom into before and after. The horde closed the river, pressed the Billingsgate approaches, and was met, street by street and tide by tide, by whatever the kingdom could muster: the fleet under captains like Bootes, the yard militias, the granary corps, and at the last, when it became clear the King himself would never be caught above ground, the volunteers of the sewer campaign.

The blockade winter broke the horde's supply; the retaking of Longmarsh broke its confidence; and what happened in the tunnels in the war's final spring broke the King, in ways the crown never published and the runners never told.

The peace has held a generation. Its monuments are strange and scattered: a brass plate at Billingsgate with a number and no names, a memorial window at St. Gertrude's that took four years to include everyone it should, and a habit, in certain cats east of the wall, of leaving a corner of the plate untouched. The ton dances harder than its grandparents did. Cats who study such things believe the two facts are one fact.

entities.title: The Sewer Campaign
entities.content:
In the war's last spring, when the horde had been beaten everywhere above ground and the King had gone below to wait the kingdom out, the call went into the yards of the Rookery for volunteers who knew the dark. What came forward were the runners: young cats, most of them poor, many of them nameless in any register, who went down into the tunnels in crews of four and finished the war where it had always really lived.

Almost nothing official exists about the campaign. The crown wanted the King ended, not described; the runners came up unwilling or unable to say what ending him had required; and Mayfur, once the bells had been rung, discovered that it preferred its victory without the details. There was no medal struck. There was no parade east of the wall. The runners went back to the cellars they had left, carrying whatever they carried, and the ton's gratitude lasted, the Beldam has said, about as long as the bunting.

The campaign's afterlife is Town's quietest fault line. It is why Sweep trusts nothing that smiles; it is what Otto decided to be owed for; it is the debt Captain Bootes toasts into uncomfortable rooms; and it is the reason the Reverend Mouser's memorial window took four years. The runners who survive are middle-aged now. They know each other on sight, anywhere, in any crowd, and what passes between them then is not for the Papers.

entities.title: The Pit Years
entities.content:
Before the war, and for a hard while after it, the old brewery yard in the Rookery held the pits: bare-claw fighting, technically forbidden, universally attended, where fortunes moved by lamplight and young toms with nothing else to sell sold the one thing they had. The era produced legends, cripples, and exactly one duke.

The Friar was the pits' last great champion: a black-and-white youngster of terrifying calm who fought, the old cats say, like a judge passing sentence, and who never once, in four years, ended a beaten opponent's career when a win would do. His final fight is the era's sealed chapter. The placards were burned, the wager book's page at Brindle's was ruled off in black, and the two cats who were in that ring have kept between them, for twenty years, a silence with the weight of a treaty.

What is known: the pits closed within a season, by pressure no one could trace; the Friar surfaced across the river with a war record, a crown gazette, and a new name; and a wiry black survivor of the same yards began, around the same time, to buy fish stalls with money he declined to explain. The Beldam, keeper of the era's whole truth, has released one sentence of it: two cats went into that ring, and neither of them lost, which was the whole trouble.

entities.title: The Fluffington Affair
entities.content:
The Fluffington Affair was the scandal of the comet season and remains the standard against which Mayfur measures its lesser earthquakes. The facts, as the ninth number of the Society Papers laid them out with dates and a floor plan: Lord Fluffington had reached a private understanding with Miss Henrietta Longwhisker on the fourth of the month, and a second, identically worded understanding with Miss Beatrice Bobtail on the sixteenth, and had contrived to attend both ladies through five subsequent evenings without either learning of the other.

The number appeared on a Wednesday. By Thursday his lordship's clubs were unavailable to him; by Friday the Longwhisker doors had closed, invisibly and permanently; and by the following week Mr. Bobtail had begun the patient purchase of debts that continues to this day. The two ladies, in the affair's one glorious turn, allied.

The unhealed question is the leak. The understandings were known, in each case, to fewer than six cats. Lady Whiskerdown's account was verbatim in places, quoting phrases his lordship had used in rooms with closed doors. The Duchess hunts the source still; the wager book at Brindle's keeps a page open on it; and the Papers themselves have said only, with what the ton swears is a smile in the type, that the authoress protects those who confide in her, and his lordship, gentle reader, was not the one confiding.

entities.title: The Whiskerdown Question
entities.content:
Who is Lady Whiskerdown? The question is seven years old, has its own standing page in the wager book at Brindle's, and has survived every answer proposed to it. The evidence cuts strangely. The Papers know Almeow's door traffic, which argues for Mr. Pounce; they know the fitting-room confidences, which argues for Madame Sphynx; they quote closed carriages, which argues for somebody's coach cat; and they have printed, at least four times, things said in rooms containing only cats of the first rank, which argues for a conclusion Mayfur prefers not to finish.

The eliminations are nearly as famous as the candidates. Mr. Tomlin has been ruled out by his own record of being wrong. The Duchess of Fluffington was a favourite until the ninth number ruined her son. La Gattina cannot be the authoress, connoisseurs hold, because the Papers' one consistent blind spot is the opera, on which they are always a week behind.

The deeper mystery, the one the clever cats have moved on to, is not the name but the method: the Papers are never wrong, and never sued, and never scooped, and no printer in Town will admit to setting the type. The Dowager Countess of Nalewood, asked at her own table whether she knew the answer, gave the reply that has become the question's epitaph: of course, my dears. I simply cannot for the life of me remember whether I am it.

entities.title: The Season of the Comet
entities.content:
Two springs ago a comet stood in the western sky for six weeks, and the season it presided over was, everyone agreed at the time and the records confirm, touched. The ton has always taken its omens seriously in the way it takes everything seriously, which is to say socially: the comet was received rather than observed, discussed as a guest, and blamed, before it left, for everything.

And there was much to blame. The comet season brought Princess Lilac and her delegation to the Square; it brought the first number of Lady Whiskerdown's Society Papers to Mayfur's doorsteps, an arrival cats now find impossible to believe was ever new; and it brought, in its final month, the Fluffington Affair, which the omen-minded still cite as the tail of the thing, the flick at the end.

The Reverend Mr. Mouser preached against comet-reading twice and was defeated by his own congregation, who pointed out that the year had, in fairness, been exactly as foretold. The comet is expected again, the astronomers say, in no lifetime presently walking. The ton has decided this is for the best. Town could not afford another such season, and privately hopes for one anyway.

entities.title: The Diamond Question
entities.content:
Every season the patronesses of Almeow's name a diamond: the young lady who is, by their infallible and unappealable judgment, the season's brightest ornament. Princess Lilac took the title the day she arrived, held it through the comet season without visible effort, and was expected to retire it, as diamonds do, upon her presumed brilliant marriage.

The Princess did not marry. And this season, for the first time in the institution's memory, the title is contested in open play. Miss Marigold's campaign has been a masterwork of the indirect: she has out-charmed the Princess at three at-homes, out-sat her on the sunning wall by the width of one strategic yard, and conducted, at the Frostwhisker musicale, the celebrated retreat in which she yielded the best seat with a grace so conspicuous that the yielding outshone the seat.

The ton has divided with a will. The old houses hold for the Princess, bloodline being bloodline; the sunning wall's younger stretch has gone over to Marigold entire; the wager book stands even; and the patronesses, who alone can settle it, have discovered an exquisite pleasure in not doing so. The Princess has declined to acknowledge that any contest exists. Marigold, asked directly, opened her eyes very wide and said she could not imagine competing with Her Highness, a sentence the connoisseurs rank among the finest blades ever drawn at Almeow's.

entities.title: The Theft of the Nalewood Collar
entities.content:
On the third wet night of spring, the Nalewood Collar vanished from a locked case in a locked room in the one house in Mayfur that had never been robbed, and Town enjoyed eleven days of the purest excitement it has known since the war. The facts were few and vivid: no lock forced, no window lifted, and in the mews behind the house, seen by two independent witnesses, a large cat with a ringed tail, moving, both agreed, without any hurry at all.

Brindle's made Marmalade Jack the thief by supper and the wagering was not on whether but on when. The Dowager did nothing. She declined the runners, declined the reward, declined, with particular firmness, the assistance of Mr. Tomlin, and waited, remarking to her companions that the collar had survived three centuries of countesses and would survive one adventure.

On the eleventh night it came back: case locked, room locked, and beside it a sprig of dried Highland heather, which is an apology, and, some say, a debt acknowledged. What debt a Rookery thief could owe or be owed by the oldest house in Mayfur is the question the ton was working itself toward asking when the Dowager closed the matter with one sentence at her own dinner table: the collar, she said, has been somewhere it was needed, and it is home now, and we will speak of the weather.

entities.title: The Incident at the Saucerine Bridge
entities.content:
At midnight, at the height of the present season, Lady Tabitha of Blackfriars was seen on the arched bridge of the Saucerine in conversation with a large ginger gentleman whose ringed tail made his identity a formality. The witness was, of all cats in Town, Mr. Tomlin of the Town Tabby, walking off a supper, who thus held in his paws the exclusive of his career, and, within the hour, in a development the ton finds funnier than the incident, chose not to print it.

What was said on the bridge is unknown. What was seen, per the one account Tomlin gave privately before going silent, was this: no assignation, no elopement, but an argument, conducted low and fierce, ending when the lady struck the gentleman flat-pawed across the shoulder and the gentleman bowed, in the correct form, held it, and walked away east.

Why Tomlin sat on it is its own scandal. The kind reading is conscience. The unkind reading arrived with the morning: the Duke of Blackfriars called on the Town Tabby's offices at nine, stayed four minutes, and the paper has since acquired, cats notice, a new press. Lady Whiskerdown's own number that week carried only one line the ton could attach to the affair, and it has been quoted on the sunning wall all season: some bridges, gentle reader, are for crossing, and some are for deciding not to.

entities.title: The Almeow's Admission Crisis
entities.content:
At the close of last season, the Dowager Countess of Nalewood exercised a patroness's most ancient right and put forward a name for membership at Almeow's: Sweep, of the Rookery. The rooms have not been calm since.

The case against is the whole architecture of the ton: Almeow's exists to be a wall, and a wall with a Rookery gate is, the Duchess of Fluffington's faction argues, not a wall. The case for is the Dowager's, delivered once, without notes, to a silent committee room: that the wall was defended in the war by cats it would not admit; that Sweep's ledgers are cleaner than half the room's; and that Almeow's may decline her candidate if it can first produce one member who has done Town a greater service, a challenge she left on the table like a glove.

The candidate himself is the crisis's finest irony: Sweep did not ask, does not want it, and has attended none of the proceedings, observing publicly that he has seen the refreshments. The patronesses are divided four to three and the four will not say which way. Mr. Pounce polishes the door plate daily and grieves. And the ton has slowly realised what the Dowager perhaps intended all along: that whichever way the vote falls, the question she actually posed, what was the war for, and who was it for, is now permanently inside the walls.

entities.title: The Catmint Question
entities.content:
Catmint is old in the Rookery and new in Mayfur, and the difference is the whole problem. East of the wall the mint is what it has been since the hungry years: the Beldam's mercy gone commercial, a softness for cats whose nights need softening, run by Otto with a rough code, no kittens, no debts collected in blood, that mostly holds. What has changed is the direction of trade. This season, for the first time, the mint is moving west.

The evidence is small and accumulating: a cloakroom at the Frostwhisker ball smelling of crushed green; a young gentleman asleep at the opera in a manner his friends could not laugh off; and the delicate, persistent question of certain Mayfur debts held east of the wall, at interest no bank would name, secured against things banks do not take. Lady Whiskerdown has printed the words borrowed plumage twice and the phrase a certain eastern florist once, and the readers who can parse her are watching the Fluffington coat.

The crown pretends not to see, the ton pretends not to know, and the Rookery watches the west take up its vice with an amusement so dry it rasps. The Beldam has made only one public remark on the matter, and it is quoted on both sides of the wall: mint was for cats who had nothing, she said. Cats who have everything should be more careful what they borrow.

entities.title: The Benefit for Mr. Grey
entities.content:
It began, as the season's best things do, with the ladies. Percy Grey's winter had been bad, Dr. Valerian's face at the door had been worse, and the ladies of Mayfur, who compete for the privilege of looking after the Honourable Percival the way their brothers compete at Brindle's, resolved upon a subscription benefit at the Theatre Royal: one night, all proceeds to the care of the ton's gentlest member.

The complications were two. The first was La Gattina, who did not wait to be asked, announced she would sing without fee, and thereby transformed a kind gesture into the hottest ticket in a decade. The second was pride: the Greys of Lower Gnawbury have nothing but their name, and a benefit is, however dressed, charity. It was Marmalade Jack who nearly wrecked it, arriving at the organising committee with his ears flat, and it was, of all cats, Mr. Bobtail who saved it, taking Jack aside for a conversation herring-cat to Highland-cat, the substance of which neither has repeated but which ended with Jack subscribing first, publicly, for a sum that raised eyebrows and questions Jack has declined in the same breath.

The night itself has already passed into legend: the house full to the gallery, young Lord Frisk's astonishing subscription, the Ambassador weeping frankly in the largest box, and Percy, propped in the front box in his best collar, looked after for one whole evening by the entire world at once. He wrote a poem about it. It is, of course, about the pattern of the chandelier's light, and it ends, the ladies point out to each other, on the word brother.

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 1: A Letter of Introduction
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

You do not know me. I intend to keep the arrangement one-sided.

There is a comet over Town this month, and everyone with a window has become an astronomer. Permit me to save you the neck-ache: the interesting bodies this season are all at ground level. A princess of Siam has taken the north house on Grimalkin Square with a retinue of four and a wardrobe of nothing, and was named diamond before her trunks were down, an efficiency this authoress can only admire. A certain silver lordship has begun paying court with an energy his creditors would recognise. And at Almeow's on Wednesday, Mr. Pounce turned away a viscount for the crime of arriving in last season's collar, which is the sort of justice one hopes to see more of.

Why write it down? Because Mayfur's memory is conveniently short, gentle reader, and mine is not. Consider me the account book of a Town that would rather not be kept.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 9: On a Gentleman's Arithmetic
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

This authoress has always held that a gentleman may be forgiven almost anything except carelessness with other cats' hearts, and it is therefore with regret, though not, I confess, with reluctance, that I lay the following sums before you.

On the fourth of this month, Lord F. reached a private understanding with a lady of long whiskers and excellent sense. On the sixteenth, the identical understanding, and I have reason to know the wording was identical, with a lady of Manxfield, whose family does not discuss tails and will now have something else not to discuss. Between these dates and since, his lordship has dined at both tables, danced at both balls, and kept both secrets with an economy of effort that would, applied to his debts, have made him the richest cat in Town.

To the two ladies, who learn of each other in this paragraph: madams, the fault is his, entirely, and this authoress suspects you will do more with that fact together than either could apart.

To his lordship: fourteen generations, my lord, and it comes to this.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 12: On the Subject of Myself
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

I am informed that the wager book at Brindle's now carries a standing page on the question of my identity, and that the odds this week favour a modiste, a doorman, and, I am obliged to report, a soprano who cannot be the authoress for reasons any regular reader of my opera notices will deduce.

The ton asks who I am. The ton would do better to ask why it tells me everything.

Consider, gentle reader, your own week. You spoke freely in your carriage because the coach cat is furniture. You spoke freely at your fitting because a mouth full of pins cannot repeat. You spoke freely on the sunning wall because warmth is a kind of privacy, and freely at cards because concentration is one, and freely at midnight because midnight is the greatest furniture of all. I was not hiding, madam. Sir, I was not even listening especially. Town confides in itself at every hour and is astonished, weekly, to have been overheard by Town.

I will say this once, and you may lay wagers on it with more confidence than on the rest of the page: I am one of you. That is the entire scandal.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 14: The Comet Departs
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

The comet has left us, and Town is putting itself to bed for the winter with the particular exhaustion of a season that will be lied about for years, the lies already improving.

The accounting, then, while the truth is warm. One princess arrived and conquered without appearing to move. One lordship courted in duplicate and was audited in public; his coat remains magnificent, and this authoress finds she has questions about the coat that must keep for a duller year. Two ladies were wronged in parallel and have merged, and Mayfur has not yet understood what it made when it made them allies; I have, and I am delighted. One paper was born, and has been wrong, I am proud to record, not once.

A closing word to the debutantes retiring to the country: you were told the season would change your lives, and it did not, and you are ashamed. Do not be. The season is a wheel, my dears. It comes around again, and the trick is not to shine the first time. The trick is to still be interesting the third.

Until the spring, gentle reader.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 17: The Season Opens
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

We are returned. The knockers are back on the doors, the sunning wall has resumed its parliament, and the Dowager Countess of N. wore the collar to the opening ball, seventeen pearls and three centuries, and the season, as is constitutionally required, thereby began.

The early intelligence. The ward of a certain black-and-white Grace has returned from the country with her ribbon, her eyes, and, this authoress suspects, a plan of campaign that would impress a field marshal; the incumbent diamond has returned with her voice and her records intact; and the two are to share a Town of finite ballrooms, which is the best news this paper has had in a twelvemonth.

Also returned: a certain ginger gentleman, seen at Billingsgate before dawn shaking paws east of the wall. Also not returned: the money of a certain silver lordship, though the coat, remarkably, persists in its glory. And at Almeow's, the patronesses convene Thursday on the gravest question ever put to them, of which this paper will say only: the candidate has cleaner ledgers than his judges, and the Dowager knows it, and so, now, do you.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 19: On a Locked Room
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

The Nalewood Collar is gone. I print it plainly because the whispered versions are already worse, and because the facts deserve better handling than they are getting at Brindle's, where a book was opened before the Dowager's household had finished breakfast, which even for that institution is brisk.

The facts: a locked case, a locked room, a house never robbed in living memory, and no mark on any of it. Two witnesses place a large gentleman with a ringed tail in the mews, and the wagering has done its arithmetic aloud. This authoress will do hers in silence, and offers the book's subscribers three observations gratis. First: the gentleman in question has never in his career taken anything whose loss would grieve a cat he respects, and his respects, though eccentrically distributed, are known. Second: the house was not entered by any means its locks were built to argue with, and there are perhaps three sets of paws in Town with that particular education, and one of them is dead. Third: the Dowager has declined the runners, declined the reward, and is, my sources agree, not in the least alarmed.

A lady who has lost three centuries of pearls does not decline help, gentle reader. Unless the pearls are not lost.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 20: The Collar Comes Home
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

The collar is home. Eleven nights abroad, returned as it went, through locks that did not notice, into a case that never learned it had been empty, and beside it, my sources are unanimous, a sprig of dried heather, which cats of the Highlands will tell you is an apology, and cats of longer memory will tell you is a receipt.

Brindle's wishes to know who. This authoress finds herself occupied by a better question: why does a cat who can walk through the oldest locks in Mayfur take a treasure he then returns? Not for profit; the collar never reached a fence, and I would know. Not for spite; the heather forbids it. Which leaves need, gentle reader: eleven days of need, somewhere, that seventeen pearls and three centuries could answer, and then come home.

The Dowager has closed the matter, and this paper, which closes nothing, will on this occasion honour the decree, for its own reasons. I will note only what she said at her table, since it deserves the permanence of type: the collar has been somewhere it was needed, and it is home now, and we will speak of the weather.

We will speak of the weather, gentle reader. But I will keep the receipt.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 22: In Praise of a Needle
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

A short number this week, Town having behaved itself, an outrage I trust will not be repeated.

Let us therefore praise Madame Sphynx. The ton brings that lady its bodies and its secrets in the same hour, and she fits the one and files the other, and in ten years on Ribbon Row not a single confidence has left her atelier by any door this authoress watches, and I watch them all. Asked again this season whether she is myself, Madame replied that a modiste who printed what she heard would lose her clients, and thereby her hearing, and what kind of fool dismantles her own loom. It is the most sensible thing said in Mayfur this year, and I commend it to the gentlemen of Brindle's, who have never once asked what Lady Whiskerdown stands to lose, and might learn something from the arithmetic.

Also this week: young Lord F. has been readmitted to the Theatre Royal on his solemn oath regarding the chandelier, which the management has accepted, and insured against.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 24: On Bridges
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

You will have heard that something occurred at midnight on the Saucerine bridge. You will have heard it because everyone has heard it, and everyone has heard it because a great house has forbidden its discussion, and Town, presented with a locked door, always checks whether the key is under the mat.

This paper knows what occurred. This paper is not going to print it.

I am aware this will disappoint the readers who take my masthead for a promise of total war, and I owe them, if not the item, then the principle withheld with it. Here it is. This authoress prints what the ton does in its ballrooms, because ballrooms are theatres and the tickets are sold. What two cats say to each other alone at midnight, before anything has been decided, while everything is still costing them something, is not yet conduct, gentle reader. It is still choosing. I report the play. I do not report the rehearsal.

Some bridges are for crossing, and some are for deciding not to, and the difference is nobody's business until the crossing. When there is conduct, you will read it here first.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 26: One Wet Thursday
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

This authoress attended the benefit at the Theatre Royal on Thursday with every intention of reporting it in her usual manner, and finds, three drafts later, that the usual manner will not serve. You will forgive a plain account.

The house was full to the gallery. La Gattina sang unpaid and, those who know say, unequalled; the Ambassador wept without the smallest attempt at diplomacy; a young lord subscribed a sum that made his guardian sit down, and gave as his reason a kindness at a party years old, which this paper records so that the gentlemen who laugh at the boy may know what they are laughing at. And in the front box, in his best collar, sat the Honourable P.G., being looked after, for one whole evening, by the entire world at once, and looking, if I may risk my reputation for accuracy, entirely well.

One item more. The first subscription, made publicly, before the committee could open its book, came from a large gentleman whose tail this paper has had occasion to mention in other contexts. The sum raised eyebrows. The gentleman declined all questions. This authoress finds she has none.

Some weeks, gentle reader, the account book of Town shows a profit.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 28: On Borrowed Plumage
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

A question of natural history. When a bird is seen in feathers finer than its diet can explain, the naturalist does not admire the feathers. The naturalist asks what the bird has promised, and to whom.

Mayfur has lately acquired some very fine feathers. There is a coat in this Town, gentle reader, you will know it, everyone knows it, that gleams at a cost its owner's visible fortune stopped explaining two years ago. There is a smell in certain cloakrooms this season that does not come off Ribbon Row: crushed and green, sweet at the edges, familiar to any cat who has walked east of the wall with their nose working. And there is, my sources in that direction assure me, a ledger east of the wall in which certain western names now appear, at interest no bank would print, secured against things no bank would take.

I have pulled this thread twice before in these pages and been patient. I am informed, by parties who ought to know, that the parties who ought to worry know I am pulling it. Good. Let this number stand as my card, formally left: this authoress is at home to the question of the coat, and will receive.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 30: The State of the Diamond
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

Midsummer, and the diamond question stands where the wager book has it: even, and getting expensive.

An appreciation of the combatants, since we are privileged to watch them. Her Highness fights as the great bloodlines fight, by existing very beautifully in the correct location; her leap remains the finest thing at Almeow's and her contempt for the contest is itself a weapon, since nothing argues rank like refusing to defend it. The challenger fights as farms fight: early, daily, and for the warm spot. Her retreat at the musicale is already taught, I am told, by governesses. Her management of a certain ducal guardian is the finest sustained performance in Town, and the knot of her ribbon has become a language, which this paper is compiling into a grammar.

The patronesses could settle it and have discovered they prefer the theatre. This authoress declines to tip her own book, but offers the wall this much: bloodline is what you are given, gentle reader, and campaign is what you do, and Town has always said it honours the first while betting, quietly, on the second. The autumn will tell us which it believes.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Private note: before the first number
entities.content:
Tonight I begin the archive, and I want the first page to be honest, since nothing after it will be published that way.

The reason is not spite, whatever Town will decide. The reason is that I watched, this winter, a lady ruined by a story that was wrong. Everyone had a version; every version was worse than the truth; and the truth, which would have saved her, had no one to keep it. She left Town in February. The versions stayed. I found I could not stop thinking about the asymmetry: Mayfur has a thousand mouths and no memory, and a society with no memory cannot be fair, it can only be loud.

So: an account book. I will write what actually happened, dated, sourced, kept. Most of it will never be printed. The printing is the smallest part; the paper is just the tax I make Town pay for teaching me its secrets. The archive is the real work, and it is for the long run, longer, perhaps, than me.

Rules, then, before I lose my nerve. Never print what I cannot stand behind. Never sell mercy, but spend it. Protect the ones who confide; audit the ones who perform. And never, under any provocation, lie in these pages, or the whole ledger is bad and I am just another mouth.

The first number goes out with the milk on Wednesday. Let us see if Town writes back.

entities.title: Working note: the door at Almeow's
entities.content:
For the record, since half of Town now believes it: Mr. Pounce is not my source, has never been my source, and would sooner eat the list than share it. My knowledge of the door traffic comes from somewhere Pounce himself has never once looked, which is the point of it, and I will keep the particulars out of even this page, writing only enough that I, later, remember the shape: the door has two sides, and everyone watches the fashionable one.

What I owe Pounce is different and larger. In the third month of the paper he worked out something close to the truth about my methods, I still do not know exactly how much, and he chose, deliberately, to do nothing. No hint, no price, no leverage. When I tested him with a false item left where only he would find it, it never surfaced anywhere. He buried it, I believe, because he judged the paper good for the institution: the ton behaves better watched, and Almeow's profits from the behaving.

So the arrangement, unspoken and understood: I never print the list, never print the patronesses' deliberations, never touch the door itself. In seven years I have broken this once, the viscount's collar in No. 1, before the arrangement existed, and Pounce's revenge was to have my own item quoted back to me at the door, verbatim, with a bow. We understand each other, that cat and I. It is the closest thing the authoress has to a colleague.

entities.title: Handoff to myself: the Fluffington leak, where I stand
entities.content:
I am setting this down properly because I keep circling it in fragments, and if I set it down I can put it away for the winter and pick the investigation up in spring exactly where it lies. So: the state of the question, for the cat I will be in March.

The affair itself I printed and stand behind. The problem is upstream. I did not find the Fluffington story; it was given to me. Fourth night after the sixteenth: a packet under the loose brick, my oldest dead-drop, the one perhaps two living cats should know exists. Inside, both understandings, dates, and the closed-door phrases, verbatim, in a fair round hand with no signature. Every fact checked. I have never printed anything so accurate that I understood so little.

What I have since established: not the Longwhisker side (they learned from my number; their shock was real). Not the Bobtails (Beatrice's rage was unrehearsed, and her father does not leak, he forecloses). Not his lordship's valet, who cannot write a fair round hand, I have seen his market lists. Which leaves the conclusion I have been avoiding all autumn: the packet came from inside the Fluffington house, from someone educated, someone patient, and someone who knew about my brick, and the last is the true alarm. The leak is not my mystery. The address is.

Spring task, then, in order: the brick first, the hand second, the house third. And a rule until solved: nothing else from that drop gets printed unverified, however perfect it reads. Perfect is now suspicious.

entities.title: Handoff to myself: closing the comet season
entities.content:
The knockers come off the doors this week. Before I bank the fires, the open ledger, so that spring-me inherits a desk and not a drift.

Open matters, in order of weight. One: the leak, see the long note of the 28th; the brick, the hand, the house; nothing from that drop unverified. Two: the coat. The arithmetic has not worked for two years and this season it stopped even pretending; I have the grooming specialist's dawn schedule and one sighting of a brindled collector at the mews gate that I cannot yet use. Patience. The coat will still be gleaming in March, and whatever is under it will have grown. Three: the princess. Two seasons in Town, no marriage sought, no marriage avoided, dispatches east twice a season. Nobody stays for the ballrooms alone. I do not have the shape of it yet, only the certainty of a shape.

Standing assets, verified this month: the drop under the brick (compromised, use eyes only), the wall at four o'clock, the fitting-room hour, the gallery cats at the Theatre Royal, and the friend at the door, who is not a source but must be counted in any honest audit of why I know things.

And one instruction I mean absolutely, from the me of tonight to the me of March: reread the first page of this archive before the first number of spring. The rules held this season. They held because I reread them.

entities.title: Working note: what I saw at the bridge, and why it stays here
entities.content:
I know what happened on the Saucerine bridge because I was nearer to it than Tomlin was, which is a sentence I will explain to no one. This page gets the facts, the number will get the principle, and Town will get nothing, and I want to record why while the reasoning is fresh, because withholding is the part of this work that goes rotten first if unexamined.

The facts. She summoned him, not the reverse; I saw the note passed at the theatre two nights prior. The argument was about the collar. She had worked out the eleven days, roughly but rightly, and she demanded to know what the pearls had bought and for whom, and when he gave her the gentleman's answer, nothing, madam, and no one, she struck him across the shoulder and called him, I could hear it from the willows, the only honest liar in Town. He bowed and held it. She watched him the whole way east. That is all, and of course it is everything: a lady does not learn a thief's schedule out of civic feeling.

Why it stays here. Nothing has been decided on that bridge yet. They are both still choosing, and what I print becomes the choice, my type has that weight now, I have watched it happen. If I name this, her brother must act, the ton must have opinions, and two cats lose the ending they were writing. The paper reports the play. It does not reach into the rehearsal. That is the principle for No. 24, and this page is where I keep its price: the best item of my season, and it stays in the dark, and I find I am glad, which is either growth or softening, and spring will tell me which.

entities.title: Sealed note: where the collar went
entities.content:
This is the item I will never print, recorded so the archive is complete, because an account book with the best entry missing is not an account book.

The collar's eleven days: Percy Grey nearly died in the first week of April. Valerian will not say it in those words but I have the apothecary's runner's word for the night deliveries, and the Grey house sat dark and quiet for six nights while the terrace tiptoed. The treatment that turned it exists, is new, is continental, and costs more than the Grey name has seen in two generations. Jack's usual trades could not raise it in time; the eastern lenders could, against security, and there is exactly one object in Mayfur both liquid enough and quiet enough: three centuries of pearls that are never looked at between balls.

And here is the part that stops my breath, professionally speaking. The locks were not defeated. I have been to the mews; I know the house's education; Jack's is not equal to it, nobody's is. The locks were opened. The Dowager let him in, or had him let in, and took the heather afterward as what it was: a receipt between parties who understand each other. Whether she knew the purpose before or worked it out after, I cannot establish, and with her those are nearly the same thing.

So the truth of the season's great theft is that there was no theft: there was a loan, from the oldest house in Mayfur to the poorest, against pearls, for a poet's life, arranged so that neither side would ever have to be thanked. I have verified every link twice. It goes nowhere. Some entries are the archive's alone.

entities.title: Evidence file: the coat, the mint, and the collector
entities.content:
Consolidating the coat file before I leave my card in print, because once No. 28 runs, the other side tidies up, and I want my state of knowledge dated prior.

Established, two sources or better. The pomade concern was sold four years ago; the proceeds are gone. The rents are mortgaged through an intermediary who traces, three steps back, to a counting-house east of the wall. The grooming specialist is paid in coin, at dawn, by the week. And the collector I saw at the mews gate last season has a name now: he is Otto's, one of the polite ones, the kind sent while the arrangement is still friendly.

Established this month, one source, the Beldam herself, which counts double: Otto holds Fluffington paper that Bobtail knows nothing of, senior to Bobtail's in every way that matters east of the wall, and the interest is not being paid in coin. It is being paid in doors: invitations, cloakroom access, a gentleman's unremarkable presence in rooms where the mint's new customers dance. His lordship is not the trade's victim. He is its footman.

What I still lack: the customer list (I will not print names on smell alone), the terms of the paper, and the answer to the only question that matters for the season's end: what happens when Bobtail's foreclosure meets Otto's seniority. Two creditors, one coat. The Beldam thinks it ends with the coat shaved and honest. I think it ends louder, and I have begun, quietly, to prepare the number I hope not to run.

entities.title: Private note: the Dowager and the question of me
entities.content:
At the opening ball, receiving line, my turn, her paw in mine. And the Dowager Countess of Nalewood, who has not seen a face in a dozen years, held my paw one full beat past the form, and said, in her voice for two: I do so look forward to Wednesday mornings, my dear. Do be careful on the stairs.

I took the stairs to my own door that night the way one takes an examination. There is nothing wrong with my stairs. Unless one is carrying something heavy, at night, in a hurry, to reach a printer's boy. Which I have done perhaps thirty times, and been observed doing, I would have sworn, never.

I have turned it every way. She may know everything: the blind hear what we show our faces we are hiding, and she has had seven years of my sentences read to her, and prose is a face. She may know only that I am someone, some shape her ears have assembled from a thousand mornings. Or she may say something of the kind to forty ladies a season on the ancient principle that most cats are carrying something, and guilt does its own confirming.

What I know is what she does with whatever she knows: nothing. Seven years of nothing, which from her is not idleness but policy. She keeps me the way I keep the bridge, the way the Beldam keeps the pit years: Town runs on held secrets, ours is the class that does the holding, and I believe she considers me, in her way, a colleague in the trade. I find I write more carefully on Tuesdays now. It is not fear. It is having a reader.

entities.title: Sealed note: the Friar and the challenger
entities.content:
I have had the whole of it for three years, and it stays sealed, and tonight I write down why, because the why is the closest thing this archive has to a constitution.

The facts, once, plainly. The Friar's last fight was against a wiry black cat from the sewer crews, just demobbed, half-starved, fighting under no name for back-pay the crown never sent. The purse that night was rigged: the yard's owners had sold the ending, the black cat was to go down in the fourth, and neither fighter knew until the third, when the pit-master's cats crowded the exits and made it plain. What the two of them did, and the Beldam's account and the placard's torn corner agree, is stop. In the ring, mid-fight, before a full house holding rigged notes: the Friar dropped his guard, the challenger sat back on his haunches, and the two of them stared the pit down until the crowd, cheated and ashamed, went home. The pits never recovered. The owners' revenge misfired into the fire that burned the placards. The Friar took his winnings, his silence, and a commission north; the challenger took nothing, which was the only thing on offer, and has been taking nothing from anybody ever since.

Neither of them lost. The Beldam's sentence, exact. The trouble is that Town cannot hold that story: it wants a winner, and would make one, and whichever cat it crowned, the other would be diminished, and they have spent twenty years arranging never to owe each other in public.

So it stays sealed, with this addendum for whoever inherits the archive: this is not an item I failed to verify. It is verified to the last claw. It is withheld because printing it would be spending two cats' honour to purchase one morning's astonishment, and the ledger does not balance. Nothing about those two is for sale here.

entities.title: Working note: the seal-point secretary
entities.content:
Adding a name to the short file of cats I do not investigate carelessly.

When Tomlin spent his month sniffing at the delegation's dispatches, the visit that ended it took, by his housekeeper's account, four minutes, and Tomlin has not printed the word Siam since, in any context, including a review of an opera set there. I called on Tomlin myself, socially, as another of my faces, wanting to see the after-effects. He is not frightened in the ordinary way. He is frightened in the way of a cat who was shown something, calmly and precisely, and given one chance to understand it. He understood it.

My own file on the secretary, thin and carefully so. Seal-point, silent, in the Princess's service since before Town. Moves through rooms the way the Princess moves, but where hers says look at me, his says there is nothing here. The dispatch runs east are his; the roof exercises at dawn are his design, the cousins merely perform them; and once, at the theatre, during the interval crush, I watched him stand for six minutes at the exact point of the corridor from which every box door was visible at once. Professional appreciation is the honest term for what I felt.

Conclusion, provisional: the delegation is what I guessed and cannot yet write, eyes, and the Princess's marriage question is a lamp arranged to be looked at. What Siam watches here, I do not know yet. The secretary and I have noticed each other noticing. We have, I think, an understanding of the professional kind: neither of us is presently the other's assignment. I intend to keep it that way through at least the autumn.

entities.title: Working note: the grammar of the ribbon
entities.content:
Three seasons of watching debutantes and I have never seen anything like the ward of Blackfriars, and I include the Princess, who is a finished thing and therefore, professionally speaking, less interesting. Marigold is a method still compiling itself, and I have the rare privilege of documenting it live.

The knot grammar, as reconstructed from my notes. The plain bow, daily wear: no signal, all quiet. The double knot, three occasions now: worn on days she intends to be underestimated, always before a move; the musicale retreat was a double-knot day, I checked my notes by candlelight to be sure. And the trailing end, twice only, both times followed within the week by a reversal for somebody who had crossed her: the Frostwhisker girl's withdrawn invitation, the abrupt country repairs of a gentleman who had laughed at her table manners. I do not believe in coincidence at two for two; at three I will call it syntax and start a proper file.

What I cannot yet determine is the campaign's object. It is not marriage; she has diverted three suitors any farm would frame. It is not the diamond as such; the diamond is a means, I would stake the archive on it. Watch item: she has begun, this month, being kind to the Rookery porters by name, and kindness with a rota is infrastructure. Whatever she is building, it has foundations east of the wall now, and I am no longer sure the Duke is the one who was adopted.

entities.title: Reflection: the archive at mid-season
entities.content:
A quiet Sunday, the season holding its breath between numbers, and I find I want to take stock of the instrument rather than the material, the way Madame Sphynx, I imagine, sometimes sharpens shears she could perfectly well use dull for another month.

What the archive has become surprises me. I began it as evidence: facts banked against Town's lying memory. It has become something nearer to a second self, and the strangeness is this: the self in these pages is better than the one that walks around Mayfur wearing my other name. She is fairer. She writes down the exculpatory detail she was tempted to omit. She has, over seven years, argued herself out of printing eleven items the walking-around self dearly wanted to run, and every one of those unprinted pages has aged into vindication. The archive is where I keep my conscience, at the reliable address.

Method note, mid-season audit, all standing. The rules of the first page: held. The drop under the brick: eyes only, still compromised, still productive, a paradox I decline to resolve while it pays. Sources current, mercies current, the sealed pages sealed.

And one thought I keep returning to, so it goes in the book. Town believes my power is knowing things. It is not. Half of Mayfur knows things. My power is that I remember them in order, with dates, next to each other, where they can talk to one another. A fact alone is gossip. A fact beside its sister fact, ten years later, is justice, or at least the raw material. Memory with a filing system, that is the whole trick, and nobody suspects it because it sounds like housekeeping.

entities.title: To the cat who inherits this archive
entities.content:
If you are reading this page, then either I have decided to trust you, which I find hard to picture, or the stairs finally had me, which the Dowager will consider a personal vindication. Either way: welcome to the archive, inheritor. Sit down. You are holding Town's actual memory, and it is heavier than it looks.

What this is: eight years, if I finish this season, of what really happened, dated and sourced, including everything I never printed. The printed numbers were the tithe. This is the estate.

How to use it, in the order that matters. First, read the first page, the rules; they are the only part I ask you to keep on faith. Second, understand the seals: the pit years, the eleven days, the bridge. These are not items awaiting courage. They are verified truths deliberately held, each for a reason argued out on its own page, and if you print one without re-arguing the reason and winning, you are not my inheritor, you are only my burglar. Third, know that the files talk to each other; that is the whole design. Read the coat file beside the mint file beside the strongbox at Manxfield and you will see the season coming that I may not be here to write.

What I ask. Keep the accounts. Spend mercy, never sell it. Protect the confiding, audit the performing. Write down the detail that inconveniences your own theory; it is the one you will need in ten years. And remember what I learned too slowly: the power was never knowing. The power is remembering in order, where one fact can find its sister.

Town will tell you who it is, inheritor, every day, in every room, at volume. Your whole work is to be the one who was listening, and wrote it down, and kept it fair.

Yours in perfect confidence, at last,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Working note: the brick first, concluded
entities.content:
The spring task list said the brick first, and the brick is done, and I am entering the result while the failure is fresh, failure being the entry a file most needs and least gets.

Six nights of watching, spread across three weeks so that even my absences kept no pattern. The drop was quiet all six. I varied the hours, the approaches, the weather; I know that wall now the way Madame knows a client's shoulders, every soft brick and every hard shadow of it, and it yielded exactly nothing, which is itself an answer of a kind: whoever posted the packet does not use the drop as a habit. Once, then. Once, precisely, with a purpose that began and ended in a single delivery, and cats who post once and never again are not informants. They are consciences, discharging.

I have also, at last, done the arithmetic I put off all winter, on who could know the address. My count of two living cats stands, I have tested it every way I own, and both of the two are impossible, for reasons I will not put even here beyond this: I built my count on the cats who matter, because that is how the ton taught me to count. The packet says my count is wrong. Therefore the error is in the counting, not the counted, and somewhere in Mayfur there is a category of knowing I have never once entered in my books.

That sentence has kept me awake two nights, and I leave it for the cat I will be when this file opens again. The hand second, then the house. And a small vow, appended: when I find the category I failed to count, I will not be angry at it. I will apprentice myself to it. An archive that discovers a blind spot and defends it is not an archive, it is the ton with better filing.

entities.title: Working note: the hand second, and the frontier
entities.content:
The hand second, and the hand has spoken, and what it says takes the investigation to the one border I have never crossed.

Method, for the file. I have kept, as any archive worth its cabinets keeps, the season's paper crop: invitations, acceptances, regrets, the cards that cross every table in Mayfur. The Fluffington house's social hand, the one that answers its invitations, is a fair round hand. I laid the packet's pages beside three seasons of that house's cards tonight, glass in paw, and there is no arguing with the letterforms: the same schooling, the same patient terminals, the same refusal of flourish. Not his lordship's hand, which I hold samples of and which signs large and thinks small. Not her Grace's, which is fine and old-fashioned and slants like weather. The house's working hand. The hand that writes when the family has said what to write.

Which is to say: an amanuensis. A clerk, a secretary, a book-room. The packet came from the desk where that household's words are made fair, and I have known it, I think, since the phrase verbatim first troubled me a year ago: nobody quotes closed doors verbatim from memory. One copies them. The wording was identical in both understandings because the same patient hand was made to engross both, and somewhere in the engrossing, something in that hand refused.

And here the file meets the frontier. I can name every cat of consequence in Mayfur and most of the inconsequent; I have ears below stairs in three fixed places I will not write even here; but an ear is not a face. The Papers have never once been below the pavement. I cannot walk into a servants' hall and ask who keeps the books; the asking itself would be the loudest item I ever published. Above stairs cannot tell a house's dozen literate paws apart, and I am, it turns out, above stairs to the marrow, which this file obliges me to enter as what it is: not a preference. A blindness. The house third, then. But the house's third storey is the one below the ground, and my whole apparatus stops at the baize door.

entities.title: Private note: the other account book
entities.content:
Town has a second paper. Not Tomlin's, which is a first paper the way a mirror is a window. A real one, and I have spent three evenings with the two numbers of it my channels have brought me, and I am putting my conclusion here before I permit myself to print a syllable of acknowledgment, because the conclusion is larger than the acknowledgment will be.

It is called The Mews, it travels, my channels insist, with the milk, and it is written by somebody who has never in their life been wrong about a price. The prose is chalk and vinegar; the tables, and it runs tables, wage tables, arrears tables, are little engines of shame that have apparently done more for the east terrace's sculleries in one season than the pulpit of St. Gertrude's has managed in a decade. It printed the going rate for a link-boy's coat against the cost of a single ballroom candle and let the two figures sit there, unadorned, like a pistol on a table. I have read a great deal of fine writing this season. Nothing has stayed with me like the candle.

And it sees what I cannot. I have tested it, quietly, against my own knowledge, and where our territories touch, the fitting-room's front of house against its back, the club's cellar bills against its wager book, the sheet is exact. But its true country is the one my whole apparatus ends at: the kitchens, the mews gates, the area steps, the four-in-the-morning city that manufactures mine. We divide the world at the baize door, that paper and I. Between us we might be adequate.

I note, professionally, that its author and I now know of each other, in the way of lighthouses. I note, personally, and only here: for seven years I have been the only cat in Mayfur who kept the whole account, and I learn tonight that I never kept the whole account, and that the discovery delights me, which I did not expect, and which I intend to examine some quiet Sunday, because delight in this trade is data.

entities.title: Working note: the coat, concluded, and a mercy held
entities.content:
The coat file closes tonight, two years open, and it closes in the one way I never budgeted for: gently.

What I have, by the usual impossible channels. Monday the notes crossed the Manxfield drawing room twice and died in the fire, and I printed that, gladly, and stand behind every word. What I have not printed: Wednesday, before dawn, the specialist was paid and dismissed at the gate by his lordship's own paw, and by that afternoon the great silver argument of Mayfur was off, clipped to the honest cat beneath, at its owner's instruction, in his own mews, in daylight. The east's paper, which was always the coat's paper whatever name it wore, is being written off; there is nothing left to secure and nobody left to walk through doors for; and the trade that ran on his lordship's invitations has lost its footman and not yet found another.

I have held the item all week, and I want the reasoning dated, because it is the bridge principle again wearing new fur. Town will see him at the last ball, or it will not; shorn, or shrouded; that appearance is his to stage, and it is the whole of his remaining estate. If I print the clipping first, I make it a ruin. If he walks into Almeow's with it, he makes it an answer. The paper reports the play, not the rehearsal, and for once, gentle archive, the rehearsal is the bravest thing in Mayfur, and it can have its curtain.

Remaining open, carried to spring: the mint's customer list, which I will not print on smell; the question of who the trade promotes to the vacant office; and one-eared arithmetic generally, which has lost this hand and does not lose seasons. The Beldam said it would end with the coat shaved and honest. I am entering, against all my professional instincts, that the Beldam may have understated it.

entities.title: Private note: the diamond, and what the bloom said
entities.content:
The patronesses named the ward at Wednesday's ball, and Thursday morning a single lilac bloom went from the north house to Grimalkin Square's west side, no card, and Town has been decoding it since with all the success it usually enjoys. This page gets my reading, because I believe I am right and cannot prove it and a page is where such things belong.

The contest was real on one side only. Marigold campaigned, brilliantly, wanting the thing; I have three seasons of the knot grammar in my files and the diamond was, from her first at-home, an objective, if never the objective. Her Highness defended nothing, because Her Highness was never holding anything: the diamond was cover, the way the marriage question is cover, a lamp arranged to be looked at while the delegation goes about whatever a delegation of eyes goes about. To fight for the title would have been to inhabit it. She let it be taken the way a professional lets a decoy be taken: gravely, and with private satisfaction at the marksmanship.

So the bloom, no card, in the delegation's own flower. Not condolence, not condescension. One campaigner's salute to another whose campaign was real: you played a true game, mine merely resembled one, and only we two know both facts. Marigold, I am told, put it in water in her own window, where the Square could see it, which answers the salute in kind and confirms, if it wanted confirming, that the little strategist read it exactly.

What remains, and goes to the spring file: if the diamond was a lamp, what has been happening in the dark it was arranged to decorate? Two seasons, dispatches east, a secretary I do not investigate carelessly, and now no title left to attend to. The Princess's cover is spent. Whatever Siam watches in Mayfur, the watching gets harder to dress from here, and next season, I think, we all learn what the lamp was for.

entities.title: Handoff to myself: the spring ledger
entities.content:
The knockers are off, the last trunks gone east and west, and I am ruling the spring page before I bank the fires, in the manner the archive now expects of me. Open matters, in order of weight, for the cat I will be in March.

One: the leak, year two. The brick is done and told me nothing; the hand is done and told me everything except a name: the packet was engrossed by the Fluffington house's working hand, an amanuensis, a book-room, a desk I cannot reach. The house third, said the plan, and the house's truth lives below the baize door, where I have ears and no face, and the ears have limits I now know exactly. Spring-me: the answer exists. It is simply kept in a country you have never entered, in books you have never read, by cats you have never counted, and your whole year's lesson is that the not-counting was the error. Begin there.

Two: the mint. The footman is lost to the trade and the trade will re-hire; watch the first ball nights of spring, watch the cloakrooms; the list is still not printable and one-eared patience is still patience.

Three: the delegation. The lamp is spent, the cover retired undefeated, and whatever the dark was decorated for comes due. The secretary and I keep our professional truce, and I keep my professional doubts about how long.

Four: the ward. A diamond now, with foundations east of the wall and a rota of kindnesses that has begun to resemble a government. I do not know what she is building. I know that I have stopped assuming I am too old to end up living in it.

And five, entered last, reread twice. The town keeps two account books now. The other's keeper and I will never meet; lighthouses do not visit; but I have concluded, watching that sheet rule off its season two days after I ruled mine, that Mayfur's whole truth finally exists, split between two desks, in two hands, and that neither desk can read the other, and that this is either the town's great safety or its great joke, and I cannot decide which, and the not-deciding is the most interesting professional sensation I have had in years. If ever a reader arrives who can sit at both desks, gentle archive, be courteous. Show them everything. Between the two of us, whoever they are, Town would at last be known entire, and being known entire, the first page has always insisted, is the only fairness Mayfur has ever lacked.

Reread the first page before the first number. The rules held again this season. They held because I reread them.

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 31: On Double Entry
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

A short lesson in bookkeeping, the season being briefly becalmed. Single entry records what happened. Double entry records what it cost, and to whom, and any honest house, the accountants insist, requires both columns or it is not keeping books, it is keeping stories.

This authoress has been informed, by channels she declines to describe even to herself, that Mayfur has lately become an honest house: that somewhere below the level at which Town conducts its self-regard, a second account book is being kept, in another hand, concerning itself with the column this paper was never positioned to enter: what the season costs, and to whom, at the prices actually paid. I have not seen it. I am reliably assured I could not obtain it, which is the most promising thing I have heard about any publication in years.

Professional courtesy, then, extended across a distance this paper will not pretend to measure: Town is at last in double entry, gentle reader, and the audit will be the better for it. You have spent seven years asking who I am. I permit myself one season of enjoying that somewhere below your breakfast rooms, somebody may now be asking it about somebody else.

Also this week: a certain punt remains at the bottom of the Saucerine, its late occupant does not, and the paper will attend to that arithmetic when the sum is complete. It is not complete.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 32: The Venetian Breakfast
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

The Frostwhisker Venetian breakfast will be remembered as the season's finest entertainment by everyone except its hostess, its caterers, and the eleven tablecloths now at rest in a laundry the ton could not find with a map. The facts, in the order the water received them: one punt, overloaded by exactly one young lord; one fountain-side table, taken broadside; one ambassadorial hat, last seen navigating toward the carp with what witnesses describe as genuine diplomatic composure.

His Excellency laughed until assisted to a chair, which Town has decided settles the matter of offence. The matter of everything else has been referred, as such matters are, to the boy's guardian, and the guardian's face at the moment of referral has been described to this authoress by three witnesses, each of whom required a restorative afterward. The young lord is to the country, rusticated until further notice, and the ton has entered its verdict with the speed it reserves for the friendless and the nineteen: ruined, they say, for the season at least, possibly for the reign.

This paper declines to co-sign the verdict, and will say only why, in the form of a question it invites the wagering interest to sit with: what a cat overturns matters less, gentle reader, than what he rights afterward, and the season is long, and the paper's book on this particular entry remains, pointedly, open.

Also this week, and gravely: the patronesses sit Thursday on the question this paper flagged at the season's opening. The candidate's ledgers have not blushed. It remains to be seen whether the committee's can say the same. The paper will report what the room decides. The paper already knows what the war decided, and so, gentle reader, do you.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 33: What Was Said in the Room
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

You will have heard that the committee voted Thursday, and how it stood, and that it was made to sit again Friday, and how it stands now: carried, five to two, and the walls of King Street still standing, to the visible surprise of two of the five.

What turned it, since Town has invented six versions and will not like losing them: no speech. The Dowager Countess of Nalewood does not make speeches twice, and her first, delivered without notes a season ago, was already on the table like a glove nobody had found the courage to lift. On Friday she asked, instead, a question, one apiece, of the four. She asked each patroness to name, aloud, for the room's records, the service to Town by which her own family had earned its place inside these walls, and she waited. She is very old, gentle reader, and entirely blind, and she waited the way the river waits, and the room discovered that of its four answers, two were trade dressed as lineage, one was lineage dressed as trade, and one, offered last and very quietly, was a grandfather's commission in the granary corps, at which the Dowager nodded and said, that is the door, my dear. The rest of us climbed through windows and have been redecorating ever since.

The vote followed as arithmetic follows. As for the candidate: he was at his scales by four the next morning, has declined the voucher with thanks, and is reported to have observed that the fish would not weigh themselves. The refreshments of Almeow's are therefore safe from him, and he from them, and this authoress notes for the archive what the room has not yet understood it conceded: the question is inside the walls now. It was carried in on a Friday, by seven ladies and one glove, and no vote to come will ever carry it out.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 34: On Second Chances
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

Two numbers ago this paper declined to co-sign a verdict and left its book open on a certain waterlogged young lord. The book closes this week, in the paper's favour, and the ton is invited to observe how the sum was made whole, because the workings are more instructive than the answer.

The young lord did not petition his guardian, did not enlist his friends, did not, wonder of the age, write to anybody. He presented himself instead, at six in the morning, to the keepers of the Saucerine, and asked for a rake. This authoress is informed that the hat was recovered Tuesday, the boat-boy's pole Wednesday, the tablecloths made good at rates that acknowledged the difference between an accident and an inconvenience, and an apology delivered where apologies are hardest and count most, by name, to a working boy, in front of the boy's master. I am further informed, by the kind of channels the ton does not believe I have, that the accounts east of the fountain were closed, paid, and annotated before the west end had finished drafting its regrets, which is, gentle reader, the correct order of solvency, and the only one this paper has ever trusted.

His Excellency, meanwhile, has kept the hat as recovered, wet side out, on a stand in the embassy hall, where he shows it to visitors as, his phrase, the season's finest trophy of the chase. The young lord dines there Thursday. The ton, which had him ruined a fortnight ago, is already re-inviting him with the special warmth it reserves for cats it feels guilty about, and he is accepting with the good grace of a boy who has learned, at nineteen and at rake's length, the season's most expensive lesson: that Town forgives a splash, gentle reader, and remembers a repair.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 35: The Arithmetic Arrives
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

Two years ago this paper began asking a question of natural history about a certain magnificent coat. One year ago it asked more pointedly. Six numbers ago it left its card. This week, the arithmetic arrives, and it arrives, as long arithmetic always does in Mayfur, wearing herring.

The facts as they may be printed. The house of Manxfield holds paper of the silver house's, quantity understated by every version in circulation, and the season of patient purchase is over: notices have gone where notices go, through attorneys of the unhurried kind, and the ton's arithmeticians, who can spot a foreclosure through three brick walls and a dinner service, have priced the outcome and begun composing their condolences, which in Mayfur are indistinguishable from invitations.

What the arithmeticians have not priced, because they cannot see it from the west, is the second column. This paper has written before of ledgers east of the wall, of interest that is not paid in coin, and of feathers finer than any visible diet explains. It repeats none of it today, and adds one sentence only, for subscribers who know how to read a balance: when two creditors hold one asset, gentle reader, the question is never which of them collects. The question is what the asset does when it discovers it was never the debtor. It was the security.

The season has three weeks to run. The paper is at home, as it announced last month, and remains so, and its door, unlike some, has never once been mistaken for a wall.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 36: The Number I Am Glad to Run
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

For two years this paper has kept a file it expected to close in ruin, and this authoress will confess, now that the expectation is dead, that she had the ruinous number half composed. It goes unprinted. What happened instead happened Monday, at Manxfield, before some forty witnesses, and deserves better type than ruin ever gets.

The father rose, took from his strongbox the three notes the whole town has wagered on, and gave them, without one word, to his daughter. The daughter, whose curtsey to a certain lordship was once complimented seam by seam in these pages, and this paper knew what it was reporting even if the room did not, took her ally by the paw, and the two ladies, wronged in parallel and merged into the season's one indissoluble institution, walked the notes to the fire and fed them in, and Miss Bobtail said, to the room, in the voice her family reserves for weights and measures: we have discussed what his lordship's fourteen generations are worth, and have decided we should all rather learn what he is worth without them. He owes us nothing. He never did. The debt was always somebody else's idea of what we were owed.

Mayfur, gentle reader, did not recover its conversation for ten minutes, and this paper has confirmed the interval with three watches.

What the fire ends, the ton can count: a foreclosure, a season's wagering, and the most patient revenge in the herring trade's history, converted at the last instant into something the herring trade has no word for and the paper does: mercy, spent, not sold. What the fire begins is his lordship's own business, conducted, the paper hears, at his own gate, at dawn, with his own paw, and Town will see the sum of it when he chooses to be seen, and not one Wednesday before. Some accounts, this paper has always held, are settled in rooms. The best ones, it learns this week, are settled in fires.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 37: The Diamond, Decided
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

At Wednesday's ball, between the second dance and the supper interval, the patronesses did the thing they have declined all season to do, and did it, this paper must record, with the timing of professionals who have been enjoying themselves: the diamond of the season is Miss Marigold, ward of Blackfriars, of Foldingworth Farm, of the ruby ribbon, and of, this paper's files being what they are, the most patiently constructed campaign since the blockade winter.

The room's eyes went where the room's eyes go, and Her Highness, who has held the title since the day she arrived and defended it precisely never, received the news with the perfect stillness of a cat receiving confirmation, inclined her head to the new diamond by exactly the degree the occasion required, and not a fraction that could be quoted against her, and resumed her conversation with the Ambassador in the delegation's own tongue.

Thursday morning, gentle reader, a single lilac bloom was delivered to the west side of the Square. No card. Town has produced eleven readings of it by Friday, each more certain than the last. This paper offers none. It reports only that the new diamond placed the bloom in water, in her own window, facing the Square, where it stands this morning, and that the two finest campaigners in Mayfur appear to be the only two cats in it who require no translation.

The wager book at Brindle's settled at sums the committee has asked this paper not to print, and this paper, feeling the season has been hard enough on that institution, complies. The knot of a certain ribbon was observed Wednesday night to be a plain bow, daily wear, all quiet. The connoisseurs are invited to consider what it means when the signal flags come down, and the fleet, gentle reader, is still moving.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 38: The Season Closes Its Book
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

The knockers come off this week, and the season, which began with seventeen pearls at an opening ball, ended Wednesday with an entrance this paper has waited two years to report without knowing it.

Lord Fluffington came to the last ball shorn. Clipped to the plain grey cat that fourteen generations of silver had been standing on all along, wearing one good coat of the woven kind, correctly cut and nothing more, and he walked into Almeow's the way cats walk into cold water: all at once, having decided. The room took its breath. And then, gentle reader, the room, which has spent two seasons pricing that cat's plumage and one week rehearsing its condescension, surprised itself, as rooms occasionally and redeemingly do: somewhere near the mantel a paw began to tap, another took it up, and what moved through that ballroom was not applause exactly, Almeow's does not applaud, but the sound a wall makes when it decides, all in one moment, to be a door.

He danced once, with Miss Longwhisker, who asked him, the whole room straining and this paper's sources better than the room's, how he did, and received the answer the season will be remembered by: lighter, madam, and learning the weather. The Duchess departs for the country a week early, taking, her household confirms, the old portrait, and leaving, this paper suspects, a version of her son she had not met before Wednesday. The wagering interest, denied its crash, has opened a book on his prospects, and the paper notes with professional pleasure that the odds are kind.

The accounting, then, while the truth is warm. One diamond passed, gracefully. One wall breached, permanently, on a Friday, by one glove. One young lord sunk and refloated inside a fortnight. Two ladies who fed a fortune to a fire and improved on it. One coat converted into a cat. And two account books, gentle reader, ruled off on a town that believes, as it packs its trunks, that it has kept its secrets, an opinion this paper has never once corrected and never once shared.

The wheel comes around, my dears. Be interesting the third time.

Until the spring, in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN
